1 · Functional or non-functional

What it is. A functional requirement states a service the system should provide: how it reacts to a particular input, how it behaves in a particular situation. A non-functional requirement states a property of that behaviour rather than a service. The deck gives the short form on slide 8: it describes not what the software will do but how the software will do it, and it covers performance, external interfaces, design constraints and quality attributes. The boundary is not fixed. The deck's rule is that the same sentence can move between the columns with the level of detail and the degree of trust. A broad goal — “the system shall protect customer data from unauthorised access” — is an NFR; expanded into concrete steps, “log in with a password and a 6-digit SMS code”, it becomes functional, because developers must build those steps. With high trust in a component, “transactions complete within 2 seconds” stays a performance NFR; in a core where delays cannot be trusted, it becomes functional — “abort any transaction over 2 seconds and trigger an audit alert”.

Why it matters

The marker decides which kind you wrote before deciding whether it is any good. A verb the system performs is functional; a measurable property of that performance is non-functional.

Example. “The system shall record a diagnosis” is functional. “The record shall be visible to the treating doctor within 2 seconds” is non-functional.

Exam trapCalling an NFR “not really a requirement”. The deck treats it as a requirement, and says functional requirements are sometimes sacrificed to meet one.

Slide 8
“software requirement that describes not what the software will do but how the software will do it EXAMPLE: software performance requirements, software external interface requirements, software design constraints, and software quality attributes.”Slide 8

2 · The three classes: product, process, external

What it is. Non-functional requirements restrict three different things. Product requirements constrain the quality of the system itself (response time, time to learn). Process requirements constrain how the team must work (development standard, method, language). External requirements constrain the environment the system must fit (legal, economic, domain rules). The deck adds its own warning: the boundaries are not clean, and one requirement can sit under more than one heading.

Why it matters

Almost every classification question in this lesson reduces to one test: who is being constrained — the system, the team, or the world outside the project?

Example. “The system shall answer a lookup in under 2 seconds” is product. “The team shall develop the system with Scrum in two-week sprints” is process. “Patient records shall be retained as the Medical Council requires” is external.

Exam trapFiling a process requirement under product because both mention the system. The subject of the sentence is the team's way of working, not the system's behaviour.

Slide 7
“They place restrictions on – (1) The product quality being developed (response time, time to learn) – (2) The development process (development standard, language) – (3) Specify external constraints (legal, economic).”Slide 7

3 · Product requirements, and their numbers

What it is. Product requirements constrain the runtime quality of the system. The deck's examples are all measurable: availability of 99% for service X, at least 8 transactions per second, the PIN prompt issued within 5 seconds of the card entering the reader, executable code limited to 512 KB, support for both PC and Macintosh, passwords of 12 characters with four character classes. The same slide admits that one product requirement, “implemented using release 5 of library Y”, is really an organisational decision.

DomainPerformanceReliabilityOther critical NFR
ATMdispense cash and update balances within x secondsrun 24/7 across bank networksencrypt PINs, prevent unauthorised withdrawals
Air-traffic controlupdate radar positions in x milliseconds99.999% availability with instant failovera software bug must not crash the display in flight
Patient monitoringalarm immediately when heart rate or oxygen falls below the limitrun for multi-day stays without a rebootsensor accuracy that avoids false alarms and missed emergencies
Stock tradingroute, match and execute an order in under 1 millisecond99.999% uptime during trading hoursexact timestamp order under concurrency, and no unauthorised trades

Why a domain carries these. Slide 14 names the three drivers the larger system imposes: physical and hardware constraints (embedded software must match the sensors, motors and network around it), the consequences of failure (lives or large sums of money demand stricter uptime and error handling), and the operational environment (hospitals, cockpits and public kiosks face continuous use and strict regulation). Across system types the Mairiza et al. survey the deck cites finds one common core in every set: performance, security and usability. If the prompt names no domain, those three are the safe NFRs to write.

Why it matters

The domain table is the deck's answer to “give an NFR for this kind of system”. Learn one row, and you can answer for whichever domain the paper picks.

Example. In a hospital, “the ward dashboard shall refresh vital signs every 5 seconds and raise an alarm within 1 second of a reading crossing the limit” is two product requirements, both testable.

Exam trapWriting “fast” or “secure” as a product requirement. Every line on slide 19 carries a number, a unit and a condition.

Slide 19
“Performance requirement – System Y shall process a minimum of 8 transactions per second … The request for the users' PIN shall be issued within 5 seconds of the card being entered in the card reader.”Slide 19

4 · Process requirements constrain the design

What it is. Process requirements are constraints on how the system is developed. They appear when a large organisation with existing standards buys a system, and they cover development standards, methods, CASE tools and management reporting: conform to ISO 12207, use the XYZ suite of CASE tools, keep every architecture diagram in Enterprise Architect or Lucidchart, produce effort reports every two weeks, write a disaster recovery plan. They range from the specific (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148) to the general (a phased lifecycle with throwaway prototyping; Scrum with two-week sprints and bi-weekly reviews).

The deck's second half is the part exam questions like: a process requirement can rule out a design. If the language is C, the architecture cannot be object-oriented. If the contract mandates waterfall with upfront sign-off, you cannot rely on evolutionary prototyping or incremental microservices discovery. If the approved CASE tool has no threading library, the design cannot use concurrency. If ISO 26262 bans dynamic allocation, the design cannot use a garbage-collected language. If the schedule is three months with a small team, buy COTS instead of building a framework.

Why it matters

It is the one class that changes what the architects are allowed to draw, so a wrong classification costs marks in two places: the NFR question and the architecture question.

Example. “All clinical models shall be maintained in the hospital's licensed modelling tool, and every release shall pass the ISO 13485 review gate” is process. It has nothing to do with how fast the system answers.

Exam trapAnswering “process requirement” for anything that mentions a process the system supports, such as admission or discharge. Process requirements are about the development process, not a business process.

Slide 23
“Mandated Programming Languages. If a process requirement states that the system shall be written in C (a procedural language), developers cannot design an Object-Oriented (OO) architecture using classes and inheritance.”Slide 23

5 · External requirements are facts, not commands

What it is. External requirements come from the environment the system is developed and used in, and they sit on both product and process. Four sources: application-domain information (insurance, banking), organisational considerations (risk management, security and privacy policy, brand), the need to work with other systems (exchange formats, APIs), and health, safety or data-protection regulation. The deck's distinctive line is the form: external requirements are rarely written as strict “the system shall…” commands. They describe facts, standards and rules of the outside world that the software must accommodate.

DomainExternal fact (not “the system shall…”)How it affects the software
Libraryevery book carries a unique 13-digit ISBN-13catalogue and scanner support exact 13-digit validation and lookup
Medicaldiseases are classified by WHO ICD-10 codesbilling and patient records store standard ICD-10 codes for reimbursement
Aviationairports and airlines carry 3-letter and 2-letter IATA codessearch and ticketing support standard IATA lookups
Retail POSproducts carry GTIN in EAN-13 or UPC barcodes managed by GS1checkout decodes 13-digit GS1 structures the same way in every store
Accounting (Thailand)13-digit national ID checksums and statutory 7% VATinvoicing verifies the checksum, calculates 7% VAT, issues a compliant invoice
Educationnational qualification frameworks (TQF) and the 4.00 GPA scalegrading calculates GPA and formats transcripts to the accreditation rule
Why it matters

This is the class students misread most often. The question usually hands you the fact and asks what requirement follows from it.

Example. “Health facilities must report notifiable diseases to the Department of Disease Control within 24 hours” is the fact. The requirement is that the system shall submit a notifiable-disease report in the DDC format within 24 hours of diagnosis, and record the submission.

Exam trapCopying the fact and calling it a requirement. The fact stays a fact; the requirement says what the system must do with it.

Slide 24
“External requirements are rarely written as strict ‘the system shall…’ commands; instead, they describe facts, global standards, and rules in the outside environment that the software shall accommodate.”Slide 24

6 · Deriving NFRs: goal decomposition

What it is. The first of three approaches. Start from enterprise goals, decompose them into sub-goals and non-functional requirements, and keep going until you reach a statement that can be measured. Its advantage, in the deck's words, is that it gives a means of tracing NFRs back to the goal of the enterprise.

Why it matters

It answers the commonest project question: where did this requirement come from? Every NFR you write has a parent goal you can name.

Example. Hospital goal: cut missed appointments. Sub-goal: remind patients in time. NFR: a reminder is delivered at least 24 hours before the slot, to 99% of patients with a registered phone number.

Exam trapStopping at the sub-goal. “The system shall be real-time” is still a goal; the NFR is the sentence with the seconds in it.

Slide 29
“Begin with enterprise goals • Decompose into sub-goal and non-functional requirements • Until a measurable statement can be defined • Advantage – provide a mean of tracing NFRs to the goal of the enterprise.”Slide 29

7 · Deriving NFRs: concerns decomposition

What it is. The second approach, from Sommerville. Take one concern, break it into the sub-concerns that produce it, and interrogate each branch with questions until the answers become requirements. The deck's example is safety on a railway: safety produces collision, derailment and personal accident; derailment is caused by excess speed for the track conditions; excess speed produces track damage.

Why it matters

It is the opposite direction from goal decomposition: you start from what could go wrong rather than from what the business wants, which is how safety and privacy requirements usually get found.

Example. Concern: a medication error. Sub-concerns: wrong patient, wrong drug, wrong dose, wrong time. Question: how does the system know which patient is in front of the nurse? Answer: bedside barcode scan matched to the order before administration is recorded.

Exam trapConfusing the two approaches. Goal decomposition descends from an ambition to a number; concerns decomposition descends from a risk to a question, and the answer to the question is the requirement.

Slide 31
“Under what conditions can excess speed cause derailment? What does ‘excess speed’ mean in reality? What information about track damage is required by the system? How is this provided”Slide 31

8 · Five problems, three escapes

What it is. The deck names five reasons NFRs are hard to express. Some constraints belong to a design nobody has chosen yet, such as the response time after a failure. Some are subjective, such as usability and learnability, and need empirical evaluation. NFRs relate to one or more FRs, so separating them hides the correspondence while merging them hides the distinction. NFRs conflict, which is why the design ends up a set of trade-offs. And there is no rule for when an NFR is optimally met, because every solution invites a more refined one.

Three escapes follow. Write goal-oriented requirements: state the business outcome, not the metric you cannot know yet. Write ranges: a minimum acceptable value and a target. Or mark the requirement TBD and revisit it after a proof of concept, when the design decision exists.

Why it matters

If the question is “why is this NFR vague?”, the answer is one of the five. If it is “what should we do instead?”, the answer is one of the three, with the trade-off named.

Example. Too early to fix a number: “The system must keep an active admission session alive through a backend failure” (goal). Ranged: “support 500 concurrent users at minimum, designed to scale to 5,000 as the ward count grows” (min and target). Postponed: “the exact recovery time will be fixed in the architecture document after the database vendor is chosen” (TBD).

Exam trapTreating “TBD” as an excuse. It is an escape only with a named owner, a named trigger and a date, otherwise it is a missing requirement.

Slide 32
“5. No rules or guidelines for determining when NFR are optimally met. Every solution might provoke a proposal for a more refined solution.”Slide 32

9 · Objective, testable, and the six-part scenario

What it is. An NFR must satisfy two attributes. It is objective if it does not express a wish, a goal or a personal opinion. It is testable if there is some process by which it can be tested. The deck then shows how to get there: turn the vague goal into measurable quality attribute scenarios, each naming the source of the stimulus, the stimulus itself, the environment, the artifact affected, the response, and the response measure.

Why it matters

This is the single most reliable way to turn a mark-losing adjective into a mark-earning requirement, and it also gives you the test: the response measure is what an acceptance test checks.

Example. Source: the ward nurse. Stimulus: opening a patient's vital-sign chart. Environment: night shift, about 40 concurrent users. Response: the chart appears with the last 24 hours. Measure: 95% of opens under 2 seconds, none over 5 seconds.

Exam trapWriting the response as the measure. “The system responds quickly” is the response; the measure is the number and the condition attached to it.

Slide 34
“NFRs must satisfy two attributes – Objective … A NFR is objective if it does not express a wish, a goal or personal opinion – Testable … A NFR is testable if there is some process by which the requirements can be tested.”Slide 34

10 · The metric table

What it is. Six qualities, each with the metric the deck accepts for it. This is the vocabulary a marker listens for: naming the metric is often the difference between “the system should be reliable” and a score.

QualityMetric
Performanceprocessed transactions per second; response time to user input
Reliabilityrate of occurrence of failure; mean time to failure
Availabilityprobability of failure on demand
Usabilitytime taken to learn 80% of the facilities; number of errors users make in a given period
Robustnesstime to restart after a system failure
Portabilitynumber of target systems
Why it matters

Availability and reliability are not the same number, and exam questions like to test that. Availability asks whether the service is there when requested; reliability asks how often it fails.

Example. The clinic system is unavailable for no more than 3 minutes in 24 hours (availability, 99.8%). It fails on average once every 500 operating hours (reliability, MTTF = 500). Both are about the same system, and neither implies the other.

Exam trapQuoting 99.9% “uptime” for everything. Pick the metric the quality needs: a batch report is judged on time to complete, not on percentage availability.

Slide 38
“Performance – Processed transactions/second, Response time to user input … Reliability – Rate of occurrence of failure, Mean time to failure … Usability – Time taken to learn 80% of the facilities, Number of errors made by users in a given time period.”Slide 38

11 · The four that get examined in detail

What it is. Reliability constrains runtime behaviour: availability (99.8% means 998 of every 1,000 time units, or a stated 3 minutes down in 24 hours), failure rate as ROCOF (2/100 means two failures per 100 operating units), MTTF (500 means one failure every 500 units), and POFOD (0.001 means one failure in a thousand requests). Performance splits three ways: response time, throughput, and timing, where the system must poll sensors at least six times a second before the value is overwritten.

Security covers unauthorised access and integrity: access permissions changed only by the data administrator, a backup every 24 hours in a secure location, all external communication encrypted. Usability covers the interface and the interaction, measurable as entry requirements (years of experience), learning requirements, handling requirements (error rate at normal speed) and likeability.

Why it matters

These four are the ones with named metrics and named models, so they are the likeliest to be asked as “give an example with a number”.

Example. Security in the deck's own health case is role-based access control: the system shall let a doctor create, read, update and delete the diagnosis of his own patient, and an administrator shall grant that access right. Composite roles extend it, and separating administration from other rights is the separation-of-duties policy.

Exam trapAnswering security with “the system shall be secure”. Name the control: permissions, encryption, backup, retention.

Slide 45
“Availability: is the system available/unavailable for service when requested by end users? … Failure rate: how often does the system fail to deliver the service expected by end-users?”Slide 45

12 · When NFRs pull against each other

What it is. Two conflicts are named in the deck. Security against usability: more validation procedures mean more inputs and less usability. Safety against availability: a conservative fail-safe position protects the system but takes it out of service, so availability drops. The deck's banking example makes it concrete: a mistyped password or an unusual login location locks the account to protect the funds, and the real owner cannot transfer money until identity is verified.

Why it matters

The answer the marker wants is not “it depends”. It is: here is the choice, here is the criterion, here is what I gave up.

Example. A ward app that locks after 30 seconds protects patient data but interrupts the nurse mid-task. Chosen compromise: lock at 2 minutes, unlock with a badge tap, and log every chart opened. Named criterion: patient safety during rounds outweighs the extra seconds.

Exam trapListing three conflicts without deciding. The trade-off analysis, with its two decision criteria, is the marked part.

Slide 43
“There is no simple and easy way to resolve these tensions … Trade-off analysis must be performed in these conflicts using the following decision criteria – level of importance attached to the requirement and – the consequence of the change on the other requirements and the wider system goals.”Slide 43

13 · ISO 9126: quality as a chain

What it is. The deck closes with the standard model. Process quality influences internal quality, which influences external quality, which influences quality in use; the reverse arrows read “depends on”. Process measures come from ISO 15504, and the six qualities of the product model are functionality, reliability, usability, efficiency, maintainability and portability, each with a one-line question. Quality in use has its own four measures: effectiveness, productivity, safety and satisfaction — the user's outcome in the real operational environment. ISO/IEC 9126 has since been replaced by ISO/IEC 25010:2011, the SQuaRE series.

Why it matters

It gives you the vocabulary to say which layer a quality requirement belongs to, and it explains why a team with poor process still ships a product that tests well for a while.

Example. Maintainability is internal: the patient cannot see it, the developer can. Usability is external. Satisfaction is quality in use. A requirement about code review belongs to process.

Exam trapCalling maintainability a quality-in-use attribute. Users never experience it directly.

Slide 51
“functionality does it satisfy user needs? reliability can the software maintain its level of performance? usability how easy is it to use? efficiency relates to the physical resources used during execution maintainability relates to the effort needed to make changes to the software portability how easy can it be moved to a new environment?”Slide 51

14 · What the final SRS must contain project

What it is. Slide 65 lists the models the final SRS is required to contain. The counts are exact, and two qualifiers are easy to miss: the activity diagrams must include object flow, and the class diagram is built from two use case descriptions with analysis patterns applied.

ModelRequired
Use case diagram1
Use case description (detail, essential level)2
Activity diagram, including object flow2
Class diagram, from the two use case descriptions, analysis patterns applied1
Sequence diagram, one scenario from each use case description2
State machine diagram, with its description1
Deployment diagram and network model, with hardware and software specification1 + 1
UI design for the two use case descriptions, with input validation and interaction messages1

The project is marked in four parts: proposal 5 points, RE process and an example of work results at each process 5, UI design for prototyping 5, core SRS content 10, plus 5 for the paper presentation.

Why it matters

This is the only list on the page that is graded directly. A missing diagram here costs more than a misused word anywhere else.

Example. If your SRS has one activity diagram, you are short one; if it has two but neither carries object flow, you are short the qualifier. Check the pair, not the presence.

Exam trapReading the list as advice. It is a specification of the deliverable: counts, levels, and the three qualifiers in italics on the slide.

Slide 65
“Functional and business process modeling – 1 use case diagram – 2 use case description (detail, essential level) – 2 activity diagram (include object flow) … Behavioral modeling – 2 sequence diagram … – 1 state machine diagram (พร้อมคำอธิบาย) … User interface design – Create UI design for the 2 use case descriptions including input validation and user interaction messages.”Slide 65

15 · Security modelling: roles and rights

What it is. A security NFR becomes a data model before it becomes code. The deck's model is RBAC: a User holds Roles, and a Role carries Rights — the access type, create / read / update / delete. The administrator assigns users to roles and rights to roles, which is why permissions are never written on the user. The extended model adds composite roles that aggregate single roles, and separates administration from ordinary rights, so that the person who grants a right is not the person who uses it. She adds in the 19 Nov class that she will not examine this pattern — it is background for seeing how security appears in a class diagram, and she skips the detail (2:12:46). The sentence to carry away from that point is the one she gives next: an NFR must be quantified, translated into a function, and placed in a use case.

Why it matters

It is the model behind every “who may see this record” requirement, and the one security answer that can be drawn as a class diagram rather than described in prose.

Example. In the clinic: physician, nurse, receptionist and administrator are roles; “read own patients' diagnoses” is a right held by the physician role; a ward clerk who covers two jobs gets a composite role rather than two accounts.

Exam trapWriting permissions on the user. A user-level permission list cannot answer “who may do this”, and it breaks the moment someone changes job.

Slides 57–58
“The system shall allow a doctor to c/r/u/d his patient diagnos information … An admin shall provide right (access type {create, read, update, delete} for a doctor to access his patient information.”Slides 57–58

1 · Three specifications, one chain

What it is. Requirements information items come in a chain. The StRS states what the stakeholders need. The SyRS states what the system as a whole must do, hardware and people included, and fixes the interfaces between the system and its software portion. The SRS is the specification for a particular software product, program or set of programs performing certain functions in a specific environment. It defines every required capability, the conditions and constraints under which the software performs, and the intended verification approaches. The deck gives the first two an outline each. The StRS: business purpose, business scope and business overview, ending in the concept of the proposed system. The SyRS: system purpose, system scope and system overview (context, functions, user characteristics), then system requirements — including system modes and states, physical characteristics, environmental conditions, and policies and regulations. The SRS outline in clause 3 sits under these two. The deck also names the working document that precedes the SRS: a requirements definition is a text report listing the functional and non-functional requirements in outline form, defining the system's scope, optionally ranked high, medium or low, and providing the information the analysis models and later workflows need.

Why it matters

A section written into the wrong document is wrong even when the sentence is good. The chain also gives you the first paragraph of the SRS: it must agree with the SyRS and say so.

Example. “Nurses need to see a patient's appointment history at the bedside” is StRS. “The hospital information system shall expose the appointment history through the clinical portal” is SyRS. “The portal shall display the last 12 months of appointments within 2 seconds” is SRS.

Exam trapTreating the SRS as a copy of the SyRS. The SRS covers the software only, and it adds the verification approach the SyRS does not carry.

Slide 17
“The software requirements specification (SRS) is a specification for a particular software product, program, or set of programs that performs certain functions in a specific environment … the SRS should then agree with and expand upon these system requirements.”Slide 17

2 · Six ways to organise functional requirements

What it is. Nothing dictates one order, and the deck quotes IEEE 830 for six schemes that work. By feature: a telephone system's local call, call forwarding, conference call. By system mode: training, normal and emergency modes. By user class: an elevator presents different capabilities to passengers, maintenance workers and firefighters. By object: a patient-monitoring system's requirements for patients, sensors, nurses, rooms, physicians, medicines. By stimulus: an automatic landing system's sections for loss of power, wind shear, sudden roll, excessive vertical velocity. By response: a personnel system's paychecks, current employee list, and so on.

Why it matters

The scheme decides whether a reader can find anything. It is also a free mark in a question that asks how you would structure a specification.

Example. A clinic appointment system organises by feature (booking, rescheduling, cancellation, reminders) if the readers are product owners, and by user class (patient, receptionist, doctor, administrator) if the readers are the training team. Both are correct; name the reader to justify the choice.

Exam trapOrganising by database table. That is a design structure, not a requirement structure, and it hides the user's view.

Slide 13
“Different systems may have requirements organized in different ways. For examples, organizing by – Feature … – System mode … – User class … – Object … – Stimulus … – Response.”Slide 13

3 · General content: making the document findable

What it is. Before any requirement, the document identifies itself. Identification is a title plus a revision notice; together they uniquely identify the document, and the revision information may carry the project name, version, release date, approved signature, the subclauses changed in this version, and every earlier version with its date. Front matter is the table of contents, the list of figures and the list of tables. Definitions explain any word with a meaning beyond the dictionary. References list every cited document by title, report number, date and publisher, with where to obtain it, split into a Compliance section (documents whose requirements are included by citation) and a Guidance section (documents that inform but impose nothing). Acronyms are spelled out.

Why it matters

These five items are cheap marks and the first things an assessor checks. A missing revision notice means nobody can tell which copy was approved.

Example. A hospital SRS cites the PDPA as guidance on consent and the Medical Council's record-retention rule as compliance. Mixing them into one list hides which citations the software must actually satisfy.

Exam trapListing references without the compliance/guidance split. The split is the point of the section.

Slide 16
“The references information should be subdivided into – a 'Compliance' section, containing references to those cited documents containing requirements which are included by that citation and – a 'Guidance' section, containing reference to those cited documents containing information, but no requirements.”Slide 16

4 · Purpose and scope

What it is. Two short sections that frame everything after them. The purpose delineates why the software is being specified. The scope names the product or products to be produced, explains what they will do, describes the application with its benefits, objectives and goals, and stays consistent with the same statements in any higher-level specification such as the SyRS.

Why it matters

The scope sentence is the boundary of the whole document. If it names the wrong product, every later requirement is graded against the wrong subject.

Example. Scope: “This SRS covers the appointment module of the hospital information system, used by receptionists and patients. It excludes billing, which is specified in SRS-BIL-02, and the laboratory interface, which is a system requirement in SyRS-HIS-01.”

Exam trapWriting scope as a feature list. Scope says which product and which boundary; features belong under product functions.

Slide 18
“Scope – Describe the scope of the software under consideration by – a) Identifying the software product(s) to be produced by name … d) Being consistent with similar statements in higher-level specifications (e.g., the system requirements specification), if they exist.”Slide 18

5 · Product perspective: eight constraints

What it is. The first section of the product overview defines the product's relationship to everything around it. If it is an element of a larger system, relate the larger system's requirements to this product and identify the interfaces between them; a block diagram of the major elements and external interfaces helps. Then describe how the software operates within eight constraints: 1 system interfaces, 2 user interfaces, 3 hardware interfaces, 4 software interfaces, 5 communications interfaces, 6 memory, 7 operations, 8 site adaptation.

Each one has content the deck spells out. Software interfaces need the other product's name, mnemonic, specification number, version and source, plus a definition of the message content and format. Operations cover modes, interactive and unattended periods, data-processing support, and backup and recovery. Site adaptation covers the data and initialisation sequences specific to an installation, and the features that must change to fit it.

Why it matters

This is where interface requirements live. A project that skips it discovers the lab analyser's HL7 version in the last week of integration.

Example. Hardware interface: a bedside tablet with a USB barcode scanner, 1280×800. Software interface: the lab system, HL7 v2.5.1 over MLLP, message ORU^R01. Communications: hospital Wi-Fi with WPA2-Enterprise. Memory: 2 GB minimum on the tablet. Operations: unattended overnight sync. Site adaptation: ward-specific bed labels and printer names.

Exam trapAnswering “user interface” for a machine-to-machine link. User interfaces are human-computer; system interfaces are machine-machine and belong to systems integration.

Slide 19
“Describe how the software operates within the following constraints: a) System interfaces; b) User interfaces; c) Hardware interfaces; d) Software interfaces; e) Communications interfaces; f) Memory; g) Operations; h) Site adaptation requirements.”Slide 19

6 · The rest of the overview

What it is. Five sections that set up the requirements without stating them. Product functions: a summary of the major functions, organised so a first-time reader understands the list; text or a diagram, but not a design. User characteristics: education, experience, disabilities and technical expertise, written as the reasons for later requirements, not as requirements themselves. Limitations: everything that limits the supplier's options — the deck's twelve letters run regulatory policies; hardware limitations; interfaces to other applications; parallel operation; audit functions; control functions; higher-order language requirements; signal handshake protocols; quality requirements; criticality; safety and security; physical and mental considerations. Assumptions and dependencies: factors that are not design constraints but whose change would change the requirements, such as “the designated hardware will run this operating system”. Apportioning: allocating requirements to software elements, with a cross-reference table by function and element, and an explicit note where the allocation is still undefined.

Why it matters

Assumptions and dependencies are the section that saves a project: write the assumption down, and a change in it is a change to the SRS, not a surprise.

Example. Assumption: every ward has Wi-Fi coverage at the bedside. If that proves false, the tablet design changes, and the requirement to sync at the bedside becomes a requirement to sync at the nurses' station.

Exam trapWriting user characteristics as requirements (“the system shall be usable by nurses”). The section explains who the users are; the requirement belongs in the software attributes.

Slide 27
“List each of the factors that affect the requirements stated in the SRS. These factors are not design constraints on the software but any changes to these factors can affect the requirements in the SRS.”Slide 27

7 · Specific requirements, and the external interface record

What it is. The specific requirements are written to a level of detail that lets a designer design to them and a tester test against them. At a minimum the section describes every input into the software, every output from it, and every function performed in response to an input or in support of an output. Each requirement is uniquely identifiable and cross-referenced to the earlier documents it derives from. External interfaces get a fixed record of twelve fields.

What the functions section adds. For every function the deck asks for five things: validity checks on the inputs, the exact sequence of operations, responses to abnormal situations (overflow, communication failure, error handling and recovery), the effect of parameters, and the relationship of outputs to inputs. Two closing sections are easy to confuse: design constraints name external standards, regulatory requirements or project limitations that force a design, while standards compliance names the standards the product's own output must follow — report format, data naming, accounting procedures and audit tracing, with the deck's payroll example of tracing every change to salary data.

Why it matters

The twelve fields are a checklist you can apply to any interface in the project, and the exam's easiest way to ask for “the details of an interface”.

Example. Fields 3 to 6 for the lab upload: from the analyser to the portal; results within 0.01 mmol/L of the reference method; mmol/L; within 5 minutes of the sample run. Fields 10 to 12: HL7 ORU^R01 v2.5.1, MLLP framing, ends with the MLLP block terminator.

Exam trapDescribing an interface in prose and calling it specified. Without range, units and timing, the tester cannot test it.

Slide 29
“At a minimum, describe – (1) every input (stimulus) into the software system, – (2) every output (response) from the software system, and – (3) all functions performed by the software system in response to an input or in support of an output.”Slide 29

8 · Performance, usability, database

What it is. The usability section states quality-in-use requirements as measurable effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in specific contexts of use. Performance splits in two. Static numerical requirements are the number of terminals, the number of simultaneous users, the amount and type of information, sometimes filed under a separate Capacity heading. Dynamic numerical requirements are the numbers of transactions and tasks and the volume of data within stated periods, for normal and for peak load. Both must be measurable, and the deck gives the rewrite: 95% of transactions in less than 1 second, not “an operator shall not have to wait”. Logical database requirements cover the types of information used, frequency of use, access capabilities, data entities and their relationships, integrity constraints and retention.

Why it matters

This section is where Lesson 8's NFRs become SRS text, and the static/dynamic split is an easy classification question.

Example. Static: 120 receptionist terminals, 300 simultaneous users, 12 months of appointment history online. Dynamic: 95% of appointment lookups under 1 second at 50 concurrent users; 99% under 3 seconds at peak outpatient hours.

Exam trapWriting “fast” as a performance requirement, then adding “the user shall not wait” as justification. The second sentence adds no number.

Slide 32
“The performance requirements should be stated in measurable terms. For example, • 95 % of the transactions shall be processed in less than 1 second. rather than, • An operator shall not have to wait for the transaction to complete.”Slide 32

9 · Software system attributes

What it is. The attributes section states the required qualities of the product. Reliability: the factors that establish it at delivery, with the definition that a system is reliable to the degree it is operational and accessible when required. Availability: the factors that guarantee a defined level, such as checkpoint, recovery and restart. Security: protection from accidental or malicious access, use, modification, destruction or disclosure, spelled out as cryptography, retained logs, functions assigned to separate modules, restricted communication between areas, integrity checks on critical variables, data privacy. Maintainability: modularity, interfaces or complexity limits, with the warning that requirements do not belong here just because they are good design practice. Portability: the percentage of host-dependent code, a proven portable language, a particular compiler or subset, a particular operating system.

Why it matters

These are the five attributes the marker checks for, and each one has a measurable form. Uncoupled from a number, they read as wishes.

Example. Availability: 99.8% during clinic hours, with recovery within 30 minutes of a node failure. Security: role-based access, TLS 1.2+, daily encrypted backup off-site, audit log retained 5 years. Portability: the portal must run on the current and previous major browser versions, no native component.

Exam trapFiling “the code shall be modular” under maintainability without a reason. The deck's warning is that good practice is not a requirement.

Slide 37
“Maintainability - Specify attributes of software that relate to the ease of maintenance of the software itself … Requirements should not be placed here just because they are thought to be good design practices.”Slide 37

10 · Verification, and what counts as supporting

What it is. The verification section gives the approaches and methods planned to qualify the software, and the deck's instruction is that it is written in parallel with sections 3.1 to 3.10 rather than bolted on at the end. Supporting information holds sample input and output formats, cost-analysis studies, user-survey results, background, a description of the problems the software solves, and special packaging instructions. The SRS must say explicitly whether that supporting material is part of the requirements.

Why it matters

It closes the loop with Lesson 8: every requirement needs a test, and a requirement with no test method is a sentence nobody can mark.

Example. Beside the 95%-in-1-second requirement sits: “Verified by a load test of 50 concurrent users over 30 minutes, measuring the 95th percentile response time.” Beside the consent requirement: “Verified by a code review of the consent screen and a test that no record is created before consent.”

Exam trapWriting verification as a separate chapter of test cases. The deck wants the test approach beside each requirement, in the same numbering.

Slide 38
“Provide the verification approaches and methods planned to qualify the software. The information items for verification are recommended to be given in a parallel manner with the information items in (3.1 external interface - 3.10 Software system attributes).”Slide 38
Lesson 10, 94 slides

Show it to them, then draw the screens

A prototype exists to be wrong early: it finds the requirements nobody could state and the ones everyone stated wrongly. The second half of the deck turns what you learned into screens, with navigation, input and output rules you can mark.

1 · What a prototype is for

What it is. A prototype is an initial version of a software system, built to demonstrate concepts, try out design options and find further possible solutions. The deck's constraint is the important half: rapid development is essential, so that cost stays controlled and users can experiment with it early in the process.

Why it matters

A prototype is an instrument, not a product. Everything about it is decided by the question it is meant to answer.

Example. A tablet storyboard shown to five ward nurses in week three answers “is this the right task order?” for the cost of an afternoon. The same question asked after the build costs a sprint.

Exam trapCalling any early screen a prototype without saying what question it tests. The question is what determines whether it should be kept or thrown away.

Slide 5
“An initial version of a software system • Demonstrate concepts • Try out design options • Find out more possible solutions • Rapid development of the prototype is essential so that costs are controlled, and users can experiment with the prototype early in the software process.”Slide 5

2 · Elicitation and validation are two different jobs

What it is. For elicitation, the prototype lets users experiment with how the system supports their work, find areas of strength and weakness, and propose requirements that are hard to describe or understand in words. For validation, testing the prototype uncovers mistakes and missing details in the initial requirements, and users frequently realise their original expectations were inaccurate or incomplete. The deck adds that many systems now follow an evolutionary approach, where the initial version is created quickly and modified into the final system. She adds the word the deck leaves out: ownership. A user who has handled a prototype has taken part in the work, and that involvement is one of the key successes of elicitation (21:01).

Why it matters

The two jobs have different success tests: elicitation succeeds if new requirements appear, validation succeeds if wrong ones are removed.

Example. Elicitation: the nurse asks for a “today's list” view nobody had specified. Validation: the same nurse discovers that the three-step admission flow she asked for takes six clicks in the prototype, and asks for it to be collapsed.

Exam trapDescribing a prototype session as validation when no requirement was checked. Elicitation produces requirements; validation checks the ones you have.

Slide 7
“Testing the prototype often uncovers mistakes or missing details in the initial requirements. Users frequently realize their original expectations were inaccurate or missing key elements (incorrect and incomplete).”Slide 7

3 · Running a validation session

What it is. Four steps, in order. Choose prototype testers who are fairly experienced and open-minded about a new system. Develop test scenarios that cover a broad range of requirements. Execute them with the user working alone while the requirements engineer observes. Document the problems and every change the system would need.

Why it matters

The four steps are a mark scheme in themselves, and the “works alone” rule is the one people break: help from the observer hides the interface's real failure.

Example. Tester: a senior receptionist who has used two booking systems. Scenarios: book a new patient, reschedule one with an unpaid bill, cancel within 24 hours. The engineer sits behind, says nothing, and writes down every hesitation with a timestamp.

Exam trapLetting the engineer guide the user. The deck's wording is exact — the user works alone, the engineer observes and records.

Slide 8
“Choose prototype testers: users who are fairly experienced and who are open minded about the use of new system … Execute scenarios: user works alone while req. engineer observes … Document problems or some change to the system.”Slide 8

4 · Nine benefits, four of them sourced

What it is. The deck lists five benefits of its own and four it marks with an asterisk from Gordon and Bieman's “Rapid Prototyping Lessons Learned”. Its own: misunderstandings between developers and users are found and system functions clarified; incomplete or inconsistent requirements surface; feasibility and usefulness are demonstrated; the prototype becomes the basis for the production specification; and user training — the user learns the system before it exists. The starred four: improved system usability, closer to user needs, improved design quality and maintainability, and reduced development effort.

Why it matters

It answers “why spend time on something you will throw away?” in the language of the project plan: risk removed, specification improved, effort reduced later.

Example. In a clinic project the throwaway storyboard cost two days and removed a requirement for a duplicate patient record that would have cost two weeks to build and unwind.

Exam trapClaiming a prototype reduces development effort without naming which effort. It reduces rework after requirements change; it adds the prototype's own cost.

Slide 9
“Misunderstandings between software developers and users may be identified clarify system functions • May find incomplete/inconsistency requirements • Demonstrate feasibility and usefulness of the application • Prototype is a basis for writing specification for a production-quality system.”Slide 9

5 · The prototype development model

What it is. Four steps, each producing one named artefact. Establish the prototype objective, which produces a prototyping plan. Define the prototype's functionality, which produces an outline definition. Develop the prototype, producing an executable prototype. Evaluate it, producing an evaluation report.

Why it matters

The artefacts make the model examinable: name the four and you have answered the question.

Example. Objective: “decide whether nurses can record vitals on a tablet during rounds.” Functionality: vitals entry, patient scan, offline save. Artefacts: a one-page plan, a three-screen outline, a clickable prototype, and a report listing eight observed hesitations.

Exam trapSkipping step one and starting with screens. Without a stated objective the evaluation has nothing to measure against.

Slide 10
“1. Establish prototype objective — Prototyping plan 2. Define prototype functionality — Outline definition 3. Develop prototype — Executable prototype 4. Evaluate prototype — Evaluation report.”Slide 10

6 · Evolutionary or throwaway

What it is. Two approaches with opposite ends. Evolutionary prototyping is open-ended: the objective is to deliver a working system, it starts from the best-understood and highest-priority requirements, it suits systems that are hard to specify such as AI, it is part of RAD and JAD, and it is now the normal technique for web sites and e-commerce. There is often no detailed specification and sometimes no formal requirements document. Throwaway prototyping is close-ended: the objective is to validate or derive requirements, it starts when requirements are not well understood, it extends analysis to reduce lifecycle cost, it clarifies key issues and gives managers information for risk assessment, and the prototype is discarded after evaluation. Functionality may be stripped, quality relaxed and performance ignored, because it will not ship.

Why it matters

Choosing wrongly costs either a discarded system or a specification nobody can write. The test is whether the requirements are knowable in advance.

Example. An AI triage assistant: evolutionary, because the behaviour is only understood once it runs. A replacement for a lab interface with a fixed HL7 profile: throwaway, because the requirements are known and the prototype exists to confirm the edge cases.

Exam trapSaying evolutionary is modern and throwaway is old. The deck assigns each to a situation, and hardware systems are named as the throwaway case.

Slide 11
“Evolutionary prototyping (open-ended approach) - Objective: to deliver a working system to end users … Throwaway prototyping (close-ended approach) - Objective: to validate or derive the system requirements.”Slide 11

7 · The six principles of interface design

What it is. The deck's frame for every screen, form and report: layout, the arrangement of items; content awareness, how well the user understands what is shown; aesthetics, how well it appeals; user experience, whether it is easy to use; consistency, the similarity of presentation across the application; and minimal user effort, whether tasks can be done quickly.

Why it matters

Critique without a principle reads as taste. Naming the principle turns “I don't like it” into a mark.

Example. A ward screen with no title and no date on the vital-sign chart fails content awareness, not aesthetics: the nurse cannot tell whether the numbers are from this morning or last night.

Exam trapMerging consistency and minimal effort. Consistency is about sameness across screens; effort is about the number of steps.

Slide 19
“Layout of the screen, form or report • Content Awareness—how well the user understands the information contained • Aesthetics—how well does it appeal to the user • User Experience—is it easy to use? • Consistency—refers to the similarity of presentation in different areas of the application • Minimal User Effort—can tasks be accomplished quickly?”Slide 19

8 · Layout and content awareness

What it is. Layout arranges items on the screen: like items are grouped into areas, areas can be subdivided, each area is self-contained, and the areas follow a natural flow. The deck's general layout has three: a navigation area, a reports-and-forms area, and a status area. It adds a warning about flow — left-to-right and top-to-bottom is a western reading habit, and other regions may read differently. Content awareness is whether the user understands what is in front of them: titles on every interface, labels on every field within an area, menus that show where the user is and how they got there, areas that are visually discernible, and forms and reports carrying their preparation date and version number.

Why it matters

Both principles are checked in a single glance at a screenshot, which makes them the cheapest marks in a UI question.

Example. A discharge summary report with no version and no date fails content awareness even if the layout is elegant: a clinician cannot tell whether it is the current summary.

Exam trapDecorative grouping without labels. An area whose purpose is not written on it is an empty box.

Slide 23
“Include titles on all interfaces, and labels of fields within each area • Menus should show where the user is and how the user got there • Forms and reports should contain preparation date and version numbers to identify age of information.”Slide 23

9 · Aesthetics, and the two kinds of ease

What it is. Aesthetics asks for a functional, inviting, pleasing interface, built on simple minimalist design, white space for separation, a density proportional to expertise (novices prefer below 50% information density, experts above it), deliberate text design in size, capitals and serif versus sans serif, and colour that does not fight itself — the deck's example is red on blue. User experience splits into two different measures. Ease of learning is how quickly a first-time user can start: onboarding walkthroughs, real-world metaphors, contextual help, tooltips and microcopy, safe sandboxes and undo, plain language. Ease of use is efficiency for the ongoing user: clear hierarchy and navigation bars, inline validation, smart defaults and autofill, appropriate input types, undo, loading indicators, confirmation dialogs, recognisable icons with labels, thumb-sized targets. The two are why the deck allows multiple interfaces for one function: Windows Explorer for most users, the command line for experts — same capability, two designs, chosen by user class rather than by fashion.

Why it matters

The deck says the two are related but can conflict: the designer must choose whether to satisfy novices or experts. That choice is a requirement, not a preference.

Example. A ward tablet used twice per shift by the same nurses can carry dense tables and shortcuts — expert density. The same system's patient-facing booking page needs a walkthrough and one action per screen.

Exam trapUsing “user-friendly” as the finding. Name which ease: learning (a first-timer's first task) or use (an expert's hundredth).

Slide 26
“Acceptable information density is proportional to the user's expertise – Novice users prefer lower density (< 50%) – Expert users prefer higher density (> 50%) … Color and patterns (e.g., don't use red on blue).”Slide 26

10 · Consistency, and the three-click rule

What it is. Consistency lets users predict what will happen: all parts of the system work the same way, so a user who learns one portion applies it everywhere. The deck names two key areas, navigation controls within and between pages, and terminology across forms and reports. Minimal user effort is the rule that follows: interfaces should minimise the effort a task takes, and the common form is the three-click rule — from the main menu to the information, in no more than three clicks.

Why it matters

Consistency is the cheapest usability gain and the commonest defect in student projects: the same concept named three ways across three screens.

Example. “Appointment”, “booking” and “visit” on three screens for the same object is a consistency defect. Pick one term and use it in the menu, the form, the report heading and the error message.

Exam trapCounting clicks as a quality measure on its own. The deck says the number should relate to the complexity of the task and be unambiguous — three clicks that each ask a clear question beat one that asks three.

Slide 33
“A common rule is the three-clicks rule – Users should be able to go from main menu of a system to the information they want in no more than three mouse clicks.”Slide 33

11 · The design process, and use scenarios

What it is. Interface design is use-case driven, incremental and iterative, and it runs in four stages: use scenario development, then the structure of navigation and I/O layout, then the basic design elements common across the system, then prototyping and evaluation. A use scenario is one path through an essential use case, written as a simple narrative; you document the most common cases so the interface is easy for those situations.

Why it matters

Starting from screens instead of scenarios produces a beautiful interface for a workflow nobody performs.

Example. Scenario: “a patient with an unpaid bill reschedules within 24 hours.” That single path forces a warning screen, a payment link and a confirmation — three screens that no feature list would have produced.

Exam trapListing screens as the structure. The structure is which screens exist and how the user moves between them, which is the next card.

Slide 34
“Use case driven, incremental and iterative process — Use scenario development … Structure of navigation and I/O layout … Basic design elements common across the system user interface.”Slide 34

12 · Structure, standards, and prototype fidelity

What it is. The interface structure is the set of components and how they work together, drawn as a window navigation diagram. A WND works like a behavioural state machine: boxes are windows, forms, reports and buttons; arrows are transitions; a single arrow means there is no return to the calling state, a double arrow means a return is required; stereotypes name the interface type. Interface standards fix the elements common across the system: the metaphor borrowed from the real world, the objects the interface names, the actions and command language, the icons, and the templates for screens and paper forms. Prototypes then come in four increasing levels of detail: storyboard, window layout diagram, HTML prototype, language prototype.

Why it matters

The WND is the interface equivalent of the state machine, so the exam can ask for one and mark it with the same rules.

Example. From the main menu, opening “Appointments” requires a return, drawn with two arrowheads. Opening “Book” from there does not return on cancel, so it gets one arrowhead; saving does return, so that transition gets two.

Exam trapDrawing every transition with two arrowheads. The double arrow is a claim that the user must come back, and only some screens do.

Slide 40
“Windows Navigation Diagrams (WND) … Similar to a behavioral state machine … Boxes represent components (Window, Form, Report, Button) … Single arrow indicates no return to the calling state • Double arrow represents a required return.”Slide 40

13 · Evaluating an interface

What it is. The goal is to improve the design before the system is built, so evaluation happens while it is being designed, with as many people as possible looking at it. Four approaches: heuristic, comparing the design against a formal checklist of principles; walkthrough, the design team presenting the prototype to users and explaining how it works; interactive, a one-person session where the user works through the use scenarios while a team member records where they hesitate or mistake the interface; and formal usability testing, in a lab, with video and keystroke and mouse recording. The deck's restriction: interactive evaluation cannot be used with storyboards or window layout diagrams. It also states what the evaluation is judging: the requirements — complete, correct and consistent — and the UI design requirement — satisfaction against the interface structure and the interface standards.

The standard checklist is Nielsen's ten heuristics: visibility of system status; match between system and the real world; user control and freedom; consistency and standards; error prevention; recognition rather than recall; flexibility and efficiency of use; aesthetic and minimalist design; help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors; and help and documentation.

Why it matters

Choosing the method is the question: a storyboard can be judged heuristically or in a walkthrough, but only something clickable supports an interactive session.

Example. Week two, paper storyboard: heuristic review by the team and a walkthrough with three nurses. Week five, HTML prototype: interactive sessions, one nurse at a time, recording every pause.

Exam trapPrescribing formal lab testing for a hand-drawn storyboard. The fidelity of the prototype decides the method available.

Slide 52
“Interactive—the users work in a one-person session with the prototype with a project team member through the use scenarios using the real use cases … Cannot be used with storyboards and windows layout diagrams.”Slide 52

14 · Navigation, menus and messages

What it is. Navigation is how the user tells the system what to do, and it also carries the success and failure messages. Three principles: prevent mistakes, simplify recovery when they happen, and keep a consistent grammar order — File → Open, never Open → File. Controls are hardware (keyboard, mouse, touch, microphone) or software (command language, natural language, menus, direct manipulation, voice). Menus come as bars, pop-ups, drop-downs and cascades, and greyed-out commands show what is unavailable. Messages come in five kinds: error, confirmation (“Are you sure?”), acknowledgment (“Order entered”), delay (the process is running), and help. The deck's when-to-use table gives each a rule. A delay message appears when an activity takes more than seven seconds; it should let the user cancel the operation and should say how long the delay may last. Confirmation asks before an irreversible act; acknowledgment confirms afterwards; help explains, and error names both the problem and the fix.

Why it matters

Five message types is a one-line answer that scores, and the error message is the place where a student interface is most often failed.

Example. Deleting a booked appointment: a confirmation before the action, an acknowledgment with an undo, an error if the slot is already taken, and a delay message while the cancellation propagates to the reminder service.

Exam trapWriting “Error: invalid input”. The deck's crafting example asks for plain language that names the problem and the fix.

Slide 63
“Error messages — user did something that is not permitted • Confirmation messages (e.g., “Are you sure?”) • Acknowledgment messages (e.g., “Order entered”) • Delay messages — provides feedback to the user that the process is running • Help messages.”Slide 63

15 · Input design and the six validation checks

What it is. Input screens capture information accurately and simply. The data may be structured (dates, names, products) or unstructured (comments, descriptions), and the principles are online versus batch processing, capture at the source (barcode readers, OCR, magnetic stripe, smart cards), and minimising keystrokes through defaults. Controls split into free-form (text, number with automatic formatting, password that hides characters and forbids cut and copy) and selection (check boxes for several, radio buttons for mutually exclusive, list boxes, sliders). Validation runs before entry: completeness, format, range, check digit, consistency between related data, and a database check against entity and referential integrity.

Why it matters

The six checks are the standard answer to “how would you validate this form”, and the project's UI design is marked on input validation explicitly.

Example. A patient registration form: completeness — surname required; format — Thai national ID as 13 digits; range — age between 0 and 120; check digit — the 13th digit of the national ID; consistency — discharge date after admission date; database check — the national ID does not already exist under another record.

Exam trapListing validation checks without the data that fails them. Each check needs one concrete example from the screen being designed.

Slide 72
“Validation checks: – Completeness – Format (e.g. MM/DD/YYYY) – Range (e.g. a number falls within a minimum and maximum value) – Check sum digit … – Consistency — data are related – Database check — does not violate entity or referential integrity.”Slide 72

16 · Output design

What it is. Outputs are the reports the system produces. Three principles: the report's usage and frequency decide its layout; manage the information load by providing only what is needed and putting the most important information near the top; and minimise bias, especially in graphs. The types: detail reports for full information, summary reports for aggregates, exception reports for what falls outside the rule, turnaround documents that become inputs again, and graphs for visual comparison, on screen or on paper.

Why it matters

The four report types are a classification question waiting to be asked, and the exception report is the one students forget.

Example. A clinic's daily list is a detail report; monthly appointment volume a summary; patients who did not attend a turnaround document, because the sheet comes back with coded reasons that are then keyed in; the no-show rate by clinic a graph — with the axis starting at zero, or it is biased.

Exam trapCalling a chart with a truncated y-axis neutral. The deck's bias warning is about exactly that.

Slide 74
“Report usage and its frequency will affect its layout • Manage the information load in a report—provide only what is needed and place most important information near the top • Minimize bias, especially in graphical displays (charts).”Slide 74

17 · From an NFR to an acceptance criterion

What it is. The deck's final device, and the most examinable thing in it. A non-functional requirement becomes a UI requirement, then an effect on the screen design, then a Given / When / Then acceptance criterion. The four NFR families it works through are operational, performance, security, and political and cultural. A worked security row: protect card data under PCI-DSS → the screen masks the CVV, blocks caching and opens 3-D Secure in a modal → the CVV shows as dots and the OTP appears without leaving the shop's site → “Given card entry, when typing the CVV, then every character is masked.”

Why it matters

This is the bridge between Lesson 8 and the project: an NFR that never reaches a Given / When / Then is a wish with a number attached.

Example. NFR: “the ward app must be usable one-handed.” UI requirement: the primary action sits in the lower third. Effect: the “Record” button spans the bottom. Criterion: given a nurse holding a tablet in one hand, when recording vitals, then every action is reachable by the thumb of that hand.

Exam trapWriting the acceptance criterion as a restatement of the requirement. Given / When / Then names a situation, an action and an observable outcome.

Slide 87
“Non-Functional Requirements Influence on HCI and Acceptance Criteria … User Interface Requirement … Effect on Screen Design … Acceptance Criteria: – Given … When … Then …”Slide 87
Lesson 11, 38 slides

Check it, then keep it true

Validation asks whether the document describes the right software; management keeps that document true after it is approved. This is the last content lesson before the final.
