1 · Validation, verification, and what a defect is

What it is. A defect is an imperfection or deficiency in a work product that does not meet its requirements or specifications and needs to be repaired or replaced. Validation asks whether the requirements define the right software, the one users expect. Verification asks whether the document conforms to the organisation's standard and carries the characteristics of a good requirement — consistency, clarity, completeness. The deck points out that both apply at three levels: the whole specification document, the set of requirements, and an individual requirement. It also settles the standards conflict: when a company standard or term is inconsistent with a widely accepted standard, a mapping between the two is agreed and appended to the requirements document, so neither side is silently overruled.

Why it matters

The two words are the most-swapped pair in the course. This deck gives them a definition each: validation is about users, verification is about the standard and the shape of the sentence.

Example. “The system shall answer a lookup within 2 seconds” passes verification (measurable, one shall) and fails validation if the clinic actually needs it at the bedside in under 1 second.

Exam trapDefining validation as “testing”. Testing is one technique; validation is the question being answered.

Slide 5
“Validate - define the right software conforms to users need • Verify – requirements conform to organization standard, requirements good characteristics.”Slide 5

2 · Four ways to validate

What it is. The deck names four fundamental practices and nothing else: requirements review, prototyping, model validation, and acceptance testing. Each answers a different question — does the document say the right thing, does the built thing match what was meant, do the models agree with each other, and will the finished product satisfy each requirement.

Why it matters

Four names is a one-line answer, and matching a situation to the right one is the usual question.

Example. A clinic SRS in review: a checklist review finds an ambiguous sentence; a storyboard session finds a missing step; a class-to-sequence check finds a transition with no message; the acceptance test list finds a requirement nobody can test.

Exam trapAnswering “walkthrough” or “inspection” as a fifth practice. They are forms of the first one, review.

Slide 8
“Fundamental practices of requirements validation 1) requirements review, 2) prototyping, 3) model validation, and 4) acceptance testing.”Slide 8

3 · The review, and the report it leaves

What it is. Reviews are the most common means of validation: a group is assigned a brief to look for errors, mistaken assumptions, lack of clarity and deviation from standard practice, and at least one customer representative belongs to that group on a customer-driven project. Reviewers work from checklists, and a review is constituted at the end of the system definition, the system specification, the software requirements specification, a baseline for a new release, or any other step. The summary report carries: objective, scope, participants, date and time, terms and a list of defect types, the checklist, results, open issues with action and responsibility, and an explanation for every reviewed item.

Why it matters

The report is the deliverable. A review with no defect-type list and no record of who fixes what leaves nothing an auditor can check.

Example. Results are a two-dimensional table: rows are checklist items, columns are the requirements reviewed, and each cell says Pass, Fail or Notes with the reason and the fix. In the clinic review, “nurse can see history” fails with “no measurable time” and the note “rewrite with 2 seconds”.

Exam trapListing participants and date but not the defect types. The defect-type list is what makes the results comparable between reviews.

Slide 10
“Examples of topics shall be included in the review summary report – Objective of the review – Scope of the review (document under revision) – Participants (reviewed by whom) – Date, time – Terms and definition (shall have a list of defect types) – List of checklist – Review results.”Slide 10

4 · The checklist, in five groups

What it is. The deck's checklist has 38 items in five groups. Organisation and structure (1–6): adherence to documentation standards and whether the requirements give an adequate basis for design and test. Completeness and correctness (7–25): cross-references, user classes and needs, inputs and outputs, system dependencies, interfaces, life-cycle support, constraints, reliability, security, safety, privacy, timing, regulation, quality attributes. Consistency and clarity (26–31): alignment with higher-level documents, freedom from duplication and conflict, single interpretation, testability. Traceability (32–33): unique identification and a traceable source. Special issues (34–38): scope, requirements that are really design solutions, resource consumption, internationalisation.

Why it matters

It is a ready-made review script for the project, and the group names are the marker's vocabulary for “what did you check”.

Example. Applied to a clinic SRS: group 2 catches the missing privacy requirement, group 3 catches the contradiction between “notify within 1 hour” and “batch overnight”, group 5 catches a requirement that is really a design choice (“use a message queue”).

Exam trapMemorising 38 items. Learn the five group names and one example from each.

Slide 11
“Organization and Structure … Standards / Unverifiable … Completeness and Correctness … Correctness / Incomplete / Interface … Consistency and Clarity … Inconsistent / Ambiguous / Unverifiable … Traceability … Special Issues … Others.”Slide 11

5 · Four defects, and how each is rewritten

What it is. The deck works four defects and repairs each. Ambiguous: “reports within a reasonable timeframe” — “reasonable” is subjective, so it becomes a 3-second limit under a stated load. Incomplete: “delete inactive user profiles” — “inactive” is undefined and the linked data is unaddressed, so it becomes 365 days plus a rule for retaining anonymised records. Contradictory: a 15-minute logout against a 45-minute uninterrupted video, repaired by pausing the timer while the video plays. Infeasible: face and iris matching against a billion records in 0.001 ms, repaired to on-device biometrics within 500 ms.

DefectThe sentence that carries itThe repair
Ambiguous“reports within a reasonable timeframe”3.0 seconds at 500 concurrent users
Incomplete“delete inactive user profiles”365 days without login; credentials removed, anonymised records kept
Contradictory15-minute logout vs a 45-minute videotimer pauses while the video plays
Infeasiblebillion-record match in 0.001 mson-device biometrics, 500 ms
Why it matters

A review question almost always wants the pair: name the defect type, then write the sentence that removes it. The deck's four are the vocabulary.

Example. “The system shall keep patient data secure” is ambiguous (secure against what?) and incomplete (no retention rule). The repair names the controls and the period: TLS 1.2, role-based access, five-year retention.

Exam trapRewriting an ambiguous requirement by swapping one adjective for another. The repair adds a number, a condition or a named standard.

Slide 15
“Infeasible requirements: These defects demand things that are technically impossible, break physical laws, or cannot be built within budget and time boundaries.”Slide 15

6 · Prototyping as validation, and its one risk

What it is. A prototype validates the engineer's interpretation of the requirements and elicits new ones. Its advantage is that assumptions become visible: the dynamic behaviour of a user interface is easier to judge from an animated prototype than from prose or a diagram. The deck adds a consequence worth quoting: a requirement defined after prototyping has extremely low volatility, because stakeholder and engineer have agreed on something they can both see — which is why it helps for safety-critical and crucial features. The named disadvantage is that cosmetic issues or quality problems in the prototype distract users from the underlying functionality.

Why it matters

It explains why prototyping sits in the validation list at all, and gives the counter-argument for a question that asks for disadvantages.

Example. A ward tablet prototype with placeholder colours draws every comment about colour and none about the two-step medication check — the team then re-skins it in hospital colours before the second session.

Exam trapPresenting prototyping as risk-free. The deck names both the volatility benefit and the distraction cost.

Slide 16
“There are also disadvantages – These include the danger of users’ attention being distracted from the core underlying functionality by cosmetic issues or quality problems with the prototype.”Slide 16

7 · Model validation, and the eight cross-model rules

What it is. Models built during analysis are validated too. For object models, a static analysis checks that communication paths exist between objects across the class and sequence diagrams; the deck's focus is the UML set — validation among functional, structural, behavioural and architectural models. The eight rules make the functional pair checkable: every action on the activity diagram has one recorded event in the use-case description; every object on the activity diagram appears in an event; the sequences match; there is one and only one description per use case; every actor in the description appears on the use-case diagram; stakeholders may appear (check local policy); every relationship in the description is drawn; and all diagram-specific rules are enforced.

Why it matters

These eight are the page's whole argument in rule form — the models are one description seen four ways, and a mismatch is a defect in the requirements, not in the drawing.

Example. A clinic activity diagram shows “check insurance” as an action, but no event in the use-case description records it — rule 1 fails, and either the description or the diagram is wrong.

Exam trapTreating the rules as diagram syntax. They compare two documents, so a syntactically perfect diagram can still fail all eight.

Slide 20
“1. Ensure one recorded event in the flows of the use-case description for each action/activity on the activity diagram … 8. All diagram-specific rules must be enforced.”Slide 20

8 · Acceptance tests and acceptance criteria

What it is. An essential property of a requirement is that the finished product can be shown to satisfy it, so each requirement gets a planned way of verifying it. Acceptance tests do this for the way end users actually conduct business; for non-functional requirements the deck says this is difficult, and that an NFR must first be analysed and decomposed until it can be expressed quantitatively. The worked example is a patient appointment system: registration with four acceptance criteria (blank fields blocked, email format validated, verification link sent, duplicate email rejected) and check-in with four more (daily roster, one-click check-in, status turns Arrived, doctor's dashboard alerted). The deck's own artefact is the DR card — one card per requirement, listing each input with its type and length, the valid and invalid values, the output for each, and the data rule behind it. Registration's card: email String/225, password String/30. Payment's card: card number String/16, CVV String/3, expiry String/4 mm/yy, holder String/6. In the 24 Nov class she says the exam may ask you to generate acceptance criteria from the flow, by checking each function's input and data type (49:22).

Why it matters

It ties the whole course together: an NFR with no decomposed measure has no acceptance test, and a requirement with no acceptance test cannot be marked as met.

Example. “The app shall be usable one-handed” has no test; decomposed to “all primary actions within the lower third, targets at least 44 px”, the test is a screen measurement at 375 px width.

Exam trapWriting one acceptance criterion per requirement. Registration needed four, one for each way it can go wrong.

Slide 22
“Identifying and designing acceptance tests may be difficult for nonfunctional requirements • To be validated, nonfunctional requirements must first be analyzed and decomposed to the point where they can be expressed quantitatively.”Slide 22

9 · Requirements management, and requirements creep

What it is. Requirements management records and maintains the evolving requirements with their context and history, and sets procedures for defining, controlling and publishing the baseline at every level of the system of interest; the deck places it inside the project and technical processes of ISO/IEC 15288 and 12207. Requirements likely to evolve are identified and communicated to acquirer and technical community alike — its example is an interest rate set by the policy holder — and a core subset may be frozen early. Every proposed new requirement is assessed for its impact on the baseline's intent. The warning: a significant proportion of requirements will change, often because the environment changed rather than because the analysis was wrong, and uncontrolled change becomes requirements creep, with cost overrun, delay, design error, dissatisfaction or cancellation.

Why it matters

It gives the honest answer to “why manage requirements”: change is inevitable, and the job is to keep it visible instead of letting it accumulate.

Example. A clinic adds “send reminders by LINE as well as SMS” three weeks before release. Managed, it is a change request with an impact on cost and test scope; unmanaged, it is creep, and the reminder test plan silently stops covering both channels.

Exam trapCalling all change a failure of analysis. The deck says much of it is an inevitable consequence of a changing environment.

Slide 29
“While changes may be unavoidable, excessive uncontrolled changes can result in “requirements creep” that can result in cost overruns, schedule delays, design errors, buyer dissatisfaction, or even cancellation of the project.”Slide 29

10 · Change management and the four baselines

What it is. Change is managed by sending every proposed change through a defined impact assessment, review and approval, backed by tracing and version control. The deck names four baselines. Functional: the reviewed system requirements, including external interface descriptions. Allocated: the reviewed system-element requirement specifications, interfaces included. Developmental: the evolving configuration at selected points in the life cycle, with change authority resting mainly with the supplier. Product: the completed system. Which baseline applies, and who may approve a change to it, is set in the project's configuration management plan. Requests arrive from problem reports, users wanting enhancements, other projects through interfaces, underlying software such as a new OS version, and senior management changing strategy. The deck's process figure walks one request through six steps: a potential change goes to the project manager, who turns it into a change request carrying its feasibility, costs and benefits; the Change Committee — client and supplier representatives — decides; the request is given a priority; the analyst updates the requirements and models, design follows, the programmer builds it, and QA verifies the changed system. The three feasibility checks are economic, technical and stakeholder satisfaction.

Why it matters

“Who may approve this change” is a different answer at each baseline, and that is the point of having four.

Example. A new clinic policy changes the cancellation window. It touches the functional baseline (a system requirement) and the product baseline (the released system), and both are approved by different people.

Exam trapNaming a single baseline for the whole project. The deck lists four and ties each to a level of authority.

Slide 30
“Functional baseline corresponds to the reviewed system requirements … Allocated baseline corresponds to the reviewed system element requirements specifications … Developmental baseline represents the evolving system … Product baseline corresponds to the completed system.”Slide 30

11 · Tracing, backward and forward

What it is. Tracing recovers where a requirement came from and predicts what a change will touch. Backward: a software requirement traces to the system requirement and the stakeholder who motivated it. Forward: a requirement traces into the requirements elaborated from it, the design entities, the implementation modules, the test cases and even the user-manual section that describes it. The traceability matrix has to be maintained for the whole life of the product; if it is not updated as requirements change, it becomes unreliable exactly when impact analysis needs it.

Why it matters

It is the mechanism behind impact analysis: without a current matrix, “what does this change touch?” can only be answered by searching.

Example. The cancellation window moves from 48 to 24 hours: backward, it traces to a board policy; forward, to one screen, two test cases and a manual paragraph — all of which must change in the same release.

Exam trapDrawing tracing as one direction. The deck defines both, and impact analysis needs the forward one.

Slide 32
“A requirement should be traceable backward to the requirements and stakeholders that motivated it … Conversely, a requirement should be traceable forward into the requirements, design entities, implementation module, and test cases that satisfy it.”Slide 32

12 · Measuring the requirements

What it is. Knowing the volume of a requirement set gives a measure of its complexity. The number is used to size a change, to estimate development or maintenance cost, or as the denominator of other measurements. The technique the deck names is functional size measurement, with two approaches: the use case point approach and the function point approach.

Why it matters

It answers “how big is this project” with something countable before a line of code exists, and it gives the change request a size as well as a direction.

Example. A clinic module with 12 use cases and 40 business rules scores one size; the “LINE reminders” change adds two use cases and three rules, so its cost is reasoned about as a proportion, not a guess.

Exam trapConfusing the volume of requirements with the size of the software. It measures the requirement set, which is what estimates are made from.

Slide 34
“Functional size measurement (FSM) is a technique for evaluating the size of a body of functional requirements. – Use case point approach – Function point approach.”Slide 34

13 · Attributes: the five groups a requirement carries

What it is. Attributes are defined, recorded and updated as the software evolves. At minimum: the classification dimensions and the verification method or acceptance-test section. Beyond that: an identifier, a summary rationale, the source, change history, risk level, dependency and priority. The deck singles one out as most important — an identifier that lets the requirement be uniquely and unambiguously identified. Its worked example groups the rest into five: identification and core data, ownership and accountability, life cycle and prioritisation, traceability links, and change control with the audit log.

Why it matters

Attributes are what make the rest of the deck possible: change management needs priority and ownership, tracing needs links, review needs the verification method.

Example. REQ-PAS-042: cancel up to 24 hours before, no fee; owner the clinic chief; priority Must; traces up to “no-shows −15%” and down to two test cases; version 2.1, changed from 48 to 24 hours by the October board.

Exam trapStopping at an ID and a description. Without the verification method and the trace links, the attribute set cannot support change or testing.

Slide 35
“The most important requirements attribute is an identifier that allows the requirements to be uniquely and unambiguously identified.”Slide 35

18 · Deployment diagrams, for the assignment

What it is. A deployment diagram is the physical view: the nodes the software runs on, the artifacts deployed to each node, and the communication paths between them. A node is drawn as a box and may carry a stereotype — «device» for hardware such as a phone or a server, «execution environment» for software that hosts other software, such as an application server or a browser. An artifact is a deployable file — the war, the jar, the database schema — and a path is labelled with its protocol: HTTPS, SQL, SMTP. It is here because the assignment needed it before the class reached it; Lesson 12, clause 9 now carries the full treatment, including the specification and instance levels.

Why it matters

It is where an NFR stops being a sentence and becomes hardware. “99.5% available” is the second application server; “card data protected” is the gateway outside the boundary and TLS on every path.

Example. The happy-fitness assignment asks for exactly this: two NFRs, then a deployment where nodes serve the member, the trainer and the assistant manager, and the card company sits outside as an external node.

Exam trapDrawing a component or class diagram and calling it deployment. A deployment diagram answers “what runs where, and over which protocol”, not “what calls what in code”.

See Lesson 12
“Elements of a deployment diagram – Nodes … – Artifacts … – Communication paths.” The 25 Nov class taught this deck; the card above is the shortest version that answers the assignment’s Q2.
Lesson 12, 42 slides

Where the software actually runs

The last content lesson, and the one the assignment asked for: physical architecture, the deployment diagram, the network model, the hardware and software specification — and the five NFRs that decide all of it.

1 · The physical architecture layer

What it is. Modern systems span two or more networked computers, and the physical architecture layer decides how the system is distributed across them and what hardware and software will be used. The deck situates it as the layer where non-functional requirements become decisions: the design, implementation and deployment must conform to the NFRs, the NFRs are both design goals and part of system acceptance, and they choose the technology — system and software architecture, hardware and software specification, and the user interface in the next lesson. Most designs are also constrained by the systems and networks that already exist.

Why it matters

It answers the question the last four lessons left open: where do these services run? Every NFR from Lesson 8 lands here as a physical decision.

Example. “The clinic must stay available during ward rounds” is not a sentence about software; it is a second application server, a load balancer and a database replica — the shape drawn in a deployment diagram.

Exam trapTreating architecture as a free choice. The deck's constraint line — existing systems and networks, plus the NFRs — removes most of the options before you start.

Slide 5
“The design, implementation, and deployment shall be conformed to the specified non-functional requirements. - NFRs will be used to set as a design goals and a part of an important system acceptance. - The selected design and implementation technology depends on the the NFRs.”Slide 5

2 · Four logics, three kinds of hardware

What it is. The deck splits architecture into software and hardware components. The software side has four logics: data storage, data access, application logic, and presentation logic. The hardware side has clients (computers, handhelds, phones), servers (mainframes, minis, micros, rack-mounted) and the networks that connect them, from dial-up to leased lines.

Why it matters

Every architecture question in this deck reduces to one move: which logic runs where. The names are just shorthand for that split.

Example. A ward tablet that only renders the chart and sends keystrokes is a thin client; the same tablet with offline recording and later sync carries application logic, so it is thick.

Exam trapNaming thin or thick by device. The label follows where the logic sits, not whether the machine is a phone or a laptop.

Slide 7
“Software components – Data storage – Data access logic – Application logic – Presentation logic … Hardware components – Clients … – Servers … – Networks.”Slide 7

3 · Server-based

What it is. In a server-based architecture the server performs all four application functions, and the client — usually a terminal with a display and a keyboard — captures keystrokes and sends them for processing. What the client cannot do, it cannot be asked to do: nothing is installed, nothing is stored, nothing is computed locally.

Why it matters

It is the architecture with the strongest control and security and the weakest scalability. The deck's table rates development cost medium — and she argues in class that even that is too low: the single central program is large, so development cost is high (17:08).

Example. A hospital's laboratory analyser console that only sends commands to a central server is server-based; the deck's classic case is the mainframe terminal.

Exam trapCalling a web application server-based because “the server does the work”. If the browser renders the interface and runs scripts, presentation and some application logic are on the client.

Slide 8
“The server performs all four application functions • The client (usually a terminal with display and keyboard) captures keystrokes and sends them to the server for processing.”Slide 8

4 · Client-based

What it is. Clients are personal computers on a network and the server is a file server on the same network. It is simple to develop, and it overloads quickly: all data is downloaded to the client for processing, network traffic becomes excessive, and the client may not have enough computing power. She adds two things the slide leaves out. A change to the application logic must be recompiled and reloaded on every client and at every site, so updates — not the first install — are the architecture's real cost (12:05). And the failure modes have named remedies: data replication, a load balancer, and data partitioning, splitting customers A–P and Q–Z across stores (12:37).

Why it matters

It is the deck's example of an architecture that works at ten users and fails at a hundred — the reason “simple to develop” is a trap rather than a recommendation.

Example. A clinic that keeps its patient database on a shared drive and installs the program on each reception PC: fine for one branch, painful when every PC pulls the whole file over the network.

Exam trapRecommending client-based for a low-cost system without naming the ceiling. The deck names three failure modes, not one.

Slide 9
“Simple to develop, but quickly overloaded – All data is downloaded to the client for processing – Network traffic may become excessive – Client may not have enough computing power.”Slide 9

5 · Client-server, thin and thick

What it is. Client-server balances processing between client and server, and it is the predominant architecture in modern systems. The amount of client processing varies: a thin client does only presentation logic, a thick client does presentation and application logic. It is highly scalable at incremental cost, and more complex because applications must be written for both sides.

Why it matters

Almost every system in the assignments is this shape, and the thin/thick choice is where the NFRs land: offline work pushes logic to the client, security pulls it back.

Example. PTSIMS with a responsive browser client is thin; a version that must record sessions offline in the gym and sync later is thick, and the sync is now an architectural requirement.

Exam trapSaying client-server is “the best architecture”. The deck lists its cost: the highest development cost of the three, because two programs have to be written.

Slide 10
“Balance processing between client and server • Predominant architecture in modern systems … – Thin clients do only presentation logic – Thick clients do presentation and application • Highly scalable at incremental cost • More complex since applications must be written for both client and server.”Slide 10

6 · Tiers: 2, 3, n

What it is. Tiers are defined by how the logic is partitioned. 2-tier: one server does data storage and access, the client does application and presentation. 3-tier: storage and access on one server, application logic on another, presentation on the client. n-tier: application logic split across two servers with data on another — common in e-commerce, better load balancing, more scalable, and harder on the network. The deck's four-tier example adds a web server in front of the application server.

Why it matters

“Which tier” is answered by which machine holds which logic — the same question as thin versus thick, counted differently.

Example. The clinic web app has a browser, a web server, an application server and a database server: four machines, four tiers, and the NFRs (availability, security) decide that the first two are separated at all.

Exam trapCounting the client as a tier in one answer and not in another. The deck counts tiers by where the logic sits and includes the client in the 2-tier and 3-tier descriptions.

Slide 11
“2-tier: one server responsible for data storage and access; client responsible for application & presentation logic – 3-tier: data storage and access logic on one server, application logic on another; client responsible for presentation logic – n-tier: application logic split among two servers, data logic on another.”Slide 11

7 · Choosing: six criteria, no winner

What it is. The process is: understand the software and hardware options, then choose among them on six criteria — cost of acquisition, cost of development, ease of development, interface capabilities, control and security, scalability. The deck's comparison makes the trade-off visible: server-based has very high infrastructure cost but medium development cost and high control, with low scalability and low interface capability; client-based has medium infrastructure, low development cost and high ease, with low control and medium scalability; client-server has low infrastructure cost but high development cost, high interface capability, medium control and high scalability.

CriterionServer-basedClient-basedClient-server
Cost of infrastructurevery highmediumlow
Cost of developmentmediumlowhigh
Ease of developmentlowhighlow–medium
Interface capabilitieslowhighhigh
Control and securityhighlowmedium
Scalabilitylowmediumhigh
Why it matters

It is the answer to “which architecture should this system use”: name the criterion the project cares about, then read the column.

Example. A clinic with no capital budget and a small team: client-server wins on infrastructure cost and scalability, and loses on development cost — which is why the NFR comparison has to name what is being traded.

Exam trapAnswering “client-server” without a criterion. The table exists precisely because each column loses somewhere.

Slide 14
“Architecture Characteristics and selection criteria … Cost of infrastructure … Cost of development … Ease of development … Interface capabilities … Control and Security … Scalability.”Slide 14

8 · Cloud, in the deck's terms

What it is. Cloud computing treats IT as a commodity on a pay-as-you-go model, with the “cloud” being the vendor's data centre and service. It is an umbrella over virtualisation (virtual rather than actual servers on shared hardware), service-oriented architectures (plug-and-play services, purchased or billed by use) and grid computing (geographically dispersed computers added or removed with load). Deployment models are private, public and hybrid; service models are IaaS (hardware: EC2, S3), PaaS (hardware plus libraries and tools: App Engine, SimpleDB) and SaaS (a complete application: Salesforce, Google Apps).

Why it matters

It is the fourth option in the architecture question, and the deck keeps the vocabulary separate from the marketing: deployment model is not service model.

Example. A small clinic runs its database on the cloud vendor's hardware but installs its own application: IaaS, public. It buys nothing on the private model; a hybrid would keep patient data private and use public storage for backups.

Exam trapMixing the axes. “Private cloud” is a deployment model; “PaaS” is a service model; a system can be private-IaaS or public-PaaS.

Slide 16
“Deployment model – Private: internal, exclusive use to the organization – Public: available to general public … – Hybrid … Service model – Infrastructure as a service (IaaS) … – Platform as a service (PaaS) … – Software as a Service (SaaS).”Slide 16

9 · The deployment diagram

What it is. A deployment diagram represents the relationships between hardware components. It has three elements and only three: nodes (any piece of hardware — clients, servers, networks, network devices), artifacts (a piece of the information system installed on a node), and communication paths (links between nodes). The deck also separates two levels: a specification-level diagram shows artifacts deployed to targets without naming instances, while an instance-level diagram names them — wsrv-01 running the web application, dbsrv-14 holding the schemas — which is how you show development, staging and production differences. Two notations finish the diagram: a node may carry a multiplicity when several identical machines run the same artifact — 2..4 «device» application servers — and the deck's extended node syntax lets UML define new node icons — workstation, server, mainframe, subnetwork cloud, database cylinder, firewall wall — while a property string such as {OS = Linux} or a named deployment specification records the node's properties.

Three ways to draw the same system, and where security sits. Slide 20 draws the Appointment System three times: (a) «Client Workstation» and «Server» stereotypes; (b) «HCI Layer», «PD Layer» and «DM Layer» artifacts inside the nodes; (c) the extended icons. All three are correct — they answer different questions: what kind of machine it is, what is installed on it, and what role it plays. Security is drawn as nodes too: a «firewall» Firewall/WAF stands between the public client and the DMZ web server, with the application and data tiers on the private network behind it.

Why it matters

This is the diagram the assignment asks for, and the deck's own phrasing is the marking vocabulary: node, artifact, communication path, and which level you drew.

Example. The PTSIMS answer from the homework is specification level; adding “wsrv-01” and “dbsrv-14” would make it instance level and show the production difference.

Exam trapPutting logic on the diagram. A deployment diagram shows hardware, what is installed on it, and the links — behaviour belongs to the sequence and activity diagrams.

Slide 17
“Elements of a deployment diagram – Nodes: any piece of hardware (e.g. client computers, servers, networks or network devices) – Artifacts: a piece of the information system which will be installed on a node – Communication paths: a communication link between the nodes.”Slide 17

10 · The network model, drawn twice

What it is. A network model depicts the major components and their geographic locations. Its purposes are to convey the complexity of the system, to show how the software components fit together, and to help specify hardware and software. The deck's method is two passes: first a top-level network model in deployment-diagram form, showing locations and how complex and costly the communication infrastructure will be; then a low-level model for each location.

Why it matters

The two-pass rule is what separates a network model from a deployment diagram: one shows geography and cost, the other shows equipment per site.

Example. A hospital with three branches and a data centre has one top-level diagram with four nodes and three links, and four low-level diagrams — one per location — each of which produces its own hardware list.

Exam trapDrawing every server in the top-level diagram. At the top level the sites are the nodes; the equipment belongs to the low level.

Slide 26
“A network diagram that depicts the major components and their geographic locations in the organization … First, create top-level network model … Second, create low-level network model for each location.”Slides 26–28

11 · Hardware and software specification

What it is. The hardware and software needed for the new application are recorded in a specification document. Software: the operating system, special-purpose software such as a DBMS, and the training, maintenance, warranties and licensing that come with them. Hardware: start from the low-level network diagram and list type and quantity of servers, peripherals, storage and backup devices; describe minimum requirements; and use an alternative matrix to evaluate vendor proposals. The deck's two samples make the scale explicit — a small-business stack for 50–500 daily users, and an enterprise stack for 50,000+ with load-balanced, auto-scaled clusters, read replicas and out-of-band management.

Why it matters

It is the third deliverable of the lesson, and it is where the architecture becomes a purchase order: quantities, minimums, and a matrix to compare vendors rather than a favourite brand.

Example. For the clinic branch in Fig. 12.2 the low-level diagram yields: one 24-port switch, one application server (16 GB RAM, 2×1 TB NVMe RAID 1), one database server (32 GB RAM), twelve client stations, and the UPS and nightly backup drive that the minimum-requirements line forces you to notice.

Exam trapWriting a specification as a wish list. The deck asks for type and quantity, minimum requirements, and a comparison matrix — three things a vendor can be held to.

Slide 33
“Hardware requirements – Use low level network diagram as a starting point – Include type & quantity of servers, peripherals, storage & backup devices – Describe minimum requirements – Use an alternative matrix to evaluate vendor proposals.”Slide 33

12 · Five NFRs and what each one builds

What it is. The deck closes with five NFRs, each carrying one requirement and the architecture it forces. Availability and reliability: 99.99% uptime — under 53 minutes a year — removes single points of failure, spreads across zones, and forces database clustering. Security and privacy: PII encrypted at rest and in transit and masked in the interface requires masking middleware in the presentation layer. Retention and compliance: seven years unalterable forces storage tiering and WORM storage. Portability: five platforms without rewriting forces containerisation and a cross-platform front end. Maintainability: a new payment gateway in under five person-days forces a decoupled, microservice architecture with creational and structural patterns.

NFRThe requirementWhat it builds
Availability99.99% uptime, ≤ 52.56 min down a yearno single point of failure; multi-zone failover; primary-replica database
Security / privacyPII encrypted in transit and at rest, masked in the UImasking middleware in the presentation layer
Retentionfinancial records unalterable for 7 yearsstorage tiering to cold storage; WORM policy
PortabilityWindows, Linux, macOS, iOS, Android, one corecontainers and orchestration; cross-platform front end
Maintainabilitynew payment gateway in < 5 person-daysdecoupled microservices; strategy and factory patterns
Why it matters

This table is the answer template for both the assignment and the exam: state the NFR as a number, then name the architectural mechanism it forces.

Example. The homework's two NFRs are rows from this table: availability gives the second application server behind the load balancer; security gives the external card gateway and TLS on every path.

Exam trapGiving the mechanism without the measure. “We will use containers” is not an answer; “portability across five platforms forces containers” is, because the requirement came first.

Slide 36
“Non-functional requirements (NFRs) act as the blueprints for a system’s quality attributes, defining how a system should behave rather than what it should do.”Slide 36

13 · A worked deployment: SookJai+ at scale

What it is. The deck's largest deployment diagram is a convenience-store chain, and it uses only the three elements. Nodes: a «device» load balancer, an application-server cluster, a database cluster in primary + replica, backup storage, four external systems (Google Cloud Identity, POS, inventory management, emailing), and a representative branch site marked ×110. Artifacts: the POS application and menu service inside the application cluster, the database inside the cluster. Communication paths: HTTPS from the branches — a «Site-to-Site VPN (HTTPS)» — and HTTPS to the four external services. The diagram is the NFRs made visible: availability forces the balancer, the cluster and the replica; security forces the VPN and the HTTPS path.

Why it matters

It is the deck's only full worked deployment at scale, and it shows how multiplicity and grouping carry scale without 110 boxes. A question that hands you a diagram like this is testing whether you can name what each node is for.

Example. The clinic group equivalent: three branches ×12 clients, one load balancer, two application servers, a primary and a replica database, nightly backup, and the lab and billing systems as external nodes over HTTPS.

Exam trapDrawing every branch as its own node. One representative node with a multiplicity is the deck's notation, and it is what keeps the diagram readable.

Slide 30
“Online Order Fulfillment System: SookJai+ … Load Balancer … Application Server Cluster … Database Cluster (Primary + Replica) … Backup Storage … Representative Branch Site ×110 … «Site-to-Site VPN (HTTPS)».”Slide 30

1 · The use-case diagram she drew the lesson around

The clinic case is now part of Lesson 6 (slides 50–62: functional requirements revisited, detail descriptions and the revised class diagram) and is referenced there. This page keeps the recording’s version because it shows the whole use-case diagram — including Communicate Real Time and Assess via Tele-Health — which the Lesson 6 deck never repeats.

Integrated Health Clinic Delivery System, from the course textbook: Dennis, Wixom & Tegarden, Systems Analysis and Design: An Object-Oriented Approach with UML, 5th ed., Wiley, Figure 4-4. Watch at 2:52:13

Reconstructed from the video frame. Three human actors, three primary use cases, two included use cases, two external systems. สร้างจากภาพในวิดีโอ: ผู้แสดงสามคน use case หลักสามรายการ use case ที่ include สองรายการ และระบบภายนอกสองระบบ

Why she showed it

  • It is the concrete form of functional requirements: each ellipse becomes a group of requirements.
  • The two «include» arrows show reuse: both scheduling paths reuse Make Appointment / Make Referral.
  • The two right-hand actors are external interface requirements, not people.

Exam use

If asked “draw a use case diagram for X”: draw the system boundary, name the human actors on the left and external systems on the right, then one ellipse per goal. Use «include» only when a step is always reused, never for optional behaviour.

2 · The same system's functional requirements

Figure 3-3B, same textbook. Watch at 2:45:00

1 · Schedule appointment

  1. Client requests to be seen by the clinic.
  2. The system displays the defined service offerings list.
  3. Client chooses an offering or requests a service-need survey so the system can decide whether it is within scope.
  4. Referral information is listed for conditions beyond scope: compare against referral list; display appropriate referrals.
  5. Appointment information is listed for in-scope conditions: real-time availability with wait time; choose an appointment time or make one in advance; calendar updated; confirmation sent.

2 · Communicate real time

  1. Client requests a real-time meeting with a caregiver.
  2. Client indicates available time and technology preference.
  3. Caregiver responds with duration and availability.
  4. Session scheduled with client and caregiver.

3 · Assess via tele-health

  1. Client answers a question matrix for suitability.
  2. Limited diagnosis developed from the answers.
  3. Diagnosis reviewed by caregiver.
  4. If minor and conclusive, diagnosis given to client; otherwise a video conference is scheduled.
Notice the pattern. These are numbered, singular, verifiable statements. That is exactly what Lesson 2 asks you to produce from a vague paragraph.

3 · PawPals — the term-project example

A dog-matching app, used to teach concept of operations, elicitation planning and feature roadmapping. Watch at 21:47

Concept of operations (ConOps)

“Thailand's first mobile application created to connect dog enthusiasts.” PawPals connects dog owners for breeding or playdates and gives them a platform to organise dog-related activities.

Value words on the slide: Trustworthy · Safety · Convenience. Those three become the non-functional themes for prioritisation.

Elicitation plan (the table to copy)

TaskSourceOwnerOutput
Interview veterinarians on breeds, health, breedingVeterinariansPM, BAInterview notes
Research competitor platformsCompetitorsBAComparison chart
Study Facebook groups for rehoming/matingFacebook groupsBAObserved user behaviour
Survey dog owners on pain pointsDog ownersPM, BAQuestionnaire + results
Research certification requirementsCertification sitesBACertification guidelines
Identify legal concerns for breeding/salesLegal/governmentBACompliance report
The exam lesson: an elicitation plan names technique, source, owner, input and output — not “do interviews”. The same structure maps directly onto the four-stage process and the twelve sources.

4 · The two other live examples

WELLJOURNEY / Wellness Connect

A student term project presented in Lesson 1: an online integrated wellness destination discovery and booking system. Watch at 2:27:28

  • AS-IS flow: discover via social media → contact provider → pay → confirmation → in-house booking management.
  • Used to show the difference between the as-is business context and the to-be system.

PickKeeper

Lesson 1, slides 13–15: “Because Every Memory Deserves the Perfect Photographer.” Watch at 25:26

  • AS-IS: photographers and customers post on Facebook/X/Instagram → private chat → payment → shoot → photos delivered.
  • Used for as-is modelling before writing requirements — five numbered steps, no software yet.

5 · What the quiz paper looked like

This is your best evidence of exam format. Watch at 2:09:49

A Word document titled Quiz-1, three pages, with numbered questions and blank space for prose. Question 10 read:

“ให้ระบุปัญหาของกระบวนการวิศวกรรมความต้องการ และแนวทางในการแก้ไขมา 2 รายการ”
State two problems of the requirements-engineering process and the approach to solving each.

So: expect “state / explain / compare / give examples” verbs, 2–4 marks each, and answers that need a named concept plus a remedy. Practise in bullet points first, then prose. The full paper, with a lesson guide and a covered model answer for each item, is in the Homework tab, together with Quiz 2.

6 · The 19 Nov class on behavioural models

From the recording, not the deck. Watch at 1:16:45

Text first, diagram second

She gives the specification to a chat model and asks it to generate PlantUML; draw.io then loads the PlantUML and renders the state machine. Her warning: part of that pipeline is not reliable yet — check the picture it produces. Two smaller tips from the same stretch: some tools number return messages for you (1, 1.1), and operation names start lowercase (searchByAuthor), the textbook’s convention.

ครูเริ่มจากเขียน specification เป็นข้อความ แล้วให้ chat model สร้าง PlantUML จากนั้นนำ PlantUML เข้า draw.io เพื่อดูภาพ state machine — แต่เตือนว่าบางขั้นของ pipeline ยังไม่เสถียร ต้องตรวจภาพที่ได้ อีกสองทิป: บางเครื่องมือใส่เลข return ให้เอง (1, 1.1) และชื่อ operation เริ่มด้วยตัวเล็ก (searchByAuthor) ตามตำรา

Bank ATM, walked end to end

Left, the high-level machine: IDLE loops on displaying a message, Insert Card → Active, Cancel or finishing → Readiness; a technician’s repair runs through Out of Service and back. Right, the fuller version: Off → self-test → IDLE, a failed self-test goes to Out of Service, and Serving Customer is a composite state with entry (read card) and exit (eject card).

แผนภาพซ้ายคือภาพระดับสูง: IDLE วนแสดงข้อความ Insert Card → Active, Cancel หรือทำงานเสร็จ → Readiness และช่างซ่อมวิ่งผ่าน Out of Service แล้วกลับมา แผนภาพขวาละเอียดกว่า: Off → self-test → IDLE, self-test ล้มเหลวไป Out of Service และ Serving Customer เป็น composite state ที่มี entry (อ่านบัตร) และ exit (คืนบัตร)

“Does the book need an unavailable state?”

A student asked. No: Checked Out and Requested by another borrower already mean the book is unavailable, so an extra state would duplicate them. She added that a third borrower can request an already-requested book — a loop — which you may store as a requested by value.

นิสิตถามว่าหนังสือต้องมีสถานะ unavailable ไหม คำตอบคือไม่ เพราะ Checked Out กับ Requested by another borrower แปลว่าไม่ว่างอยู่แล้ว การเพิ่มสถานะจะซ้ำซ้อน และถ้าคนที่สามขอหนังสือที่ถูกขออยู่แล้วจะเกิดลูป จึงอาจเก็บค่า requested by ไว้

Two corrections to the deck

She flags the guard-condition syntax on the order machine, wants “order is closed” as a state before termination, and cuts the deck’s second final state so both paths reach one stop state. Fig. 7.5 in Lesson 7 is drawn her way; the memo there carries both moments.

ครูแก้สไลด์สองจุด: guard ต้องเขียนให้ถูก syntax, “order is closed” ควรเป็น state ก่อน terminate, และตัด final state ที่สองออกให้เหลือจุดจบเดียว — Fig. 7.5 ใน Lesson 7 วาดตามคำแก้ และ memo ในบทนั้นมี timestamp ของทั้งสองช่วง

7 · The 19–20 Nov classes, beyond the decks

From the two recordings, not the slides. Watch the NFR class at 50:15 · Watch the UI class at 11:26

What “conform to ISO 12207” actually means

The deck says a process requirement can be “the development process shall conform to ISO 12207” and stops there. She opens the standard itself: it divides the software life cycle into four process clusters, and it defines a single process as Purpose → Outcome → Activity → Task (clause 6.4.2). That structure is what a team is audited against, and it is why the requirement is testable at all. 50:15 54:47

สไลด์บอกแค่ว่าต้องทำตาม ISO 12207 แล้วจบ ครูเปิดมาตรฐานจริงให้ดู: เขาแบ่ง process ของ software lifecycle เป็นสี่คลัสเตอร์ และนิยามหนึ่ง process ว่าประกอบด้วย Purpose → Outcome → Activity → Task (ข้อ 6.4.2) นี่คือสิ่งที่ตรวจได้ว่า “ทำตามมาตรฐาน” หมายถึงอะไร

A metric is a template, not a word

She shares the ISO measurement sheet. Every metric has the same six slots: name, purpose, how to apply it, how to measure it, which standard defines it, and who uses it. Then she computes one aloud — functional adequacy is 1 − A/B, and with ten functions of which one is defective, 9/10 gives 0.9. The deck prints only the one-line metric list. 1:59:20 2:00:56

ครูแชร์ตาราง metric ของ ISO ให้ดู ทุก metric มีช่องเหมือนกันหกช่อง — ชื่อ วัตถุประสงค์ วิธีประยุกต์ วิธีวัด มาตรฐานที่นิยาม และคนที่ใช้ จากนั้นคำนวณสด: functional adequacy = 1 − A/B ถ้ามี 10 ฟังก์ชันและเสีย 1 ตัว คำตอบคือ 9/10 = 0.9

Six scenarios, counted out loud

From the fragment “Patient {old/new} make {new/cancel/change}” she counts the use scenarios: two patient states times three actions is six, then adds two operations only an existing patient can perform — change own details and change the payment method — which no description had listed. Alternate flows are extra, not part of the count. In the same class she says she would write an activity diagram straight from a high-level description, before any use-case prose. 49:26 48:31

จากประโยค Patient {old/new} make {new/cancel/change} ครูนับ scenario ให้ฟัง: สองสถานะผู้ป่วยคูณสามการกระทำเท่ากับหก แล้วเสริมอีกสอง operation ที่ทำได้เฉพาะผู้ป่วยเก่า — แก้ข้อมูลตัวเองและเปลี่ยนวิธีชำระเงิน — ซึ่งไม่มีในคำอธิบายใด ส่วน alternate flow เป็นของเพิ่ม ไม่นับรวม ในคาบเดียวกันครูบอกว่าเธอเขียน activity diagram จากคำอธิบายระดับสูงก่อนก็ได้

What a prototype session must judge

Her rule for what prototype testing is for: the functions, the flow of work, whether it helps the user act — “not cosmetics, not whether it looks premium”. A prototype evaluated on colour and polish has tested nothing that belongs to requirements. 21:28

กฎของครูว่าการทดสอบ prototype มีไว้ทำอะไร: ฟังก์ชันงาน ลำดับการทำงาน และว่ามันช่วยให้ผู้ใช้ลงมือทำได้จริงไหม — “ไม่ใช่ความสวยหรือความดูหรู” prototype ที่ถูกประเมินด้วยสีและความเรียบร้อยยังไม่ได้ทดสอบอะไรที่เป็นเรื่องของ requirement เลย

Two corrections from the project demos

On a pre-operative decision-support class diagram she would split User by generalisation into administrator, surgeon and anaesthesiologist, so each role carries its own associations instead of one class holding all of them. On a pre-visit and import use case, the patient syncing a wearable and the laboratory pushing results had been written as one flow; she sends it back to the question who performs this function? — because a description that mixes the two hides both actors. 2:33:27 2:47:39

ครูแก้จากงานที่นิสิตนำเสนอสองจุด: ใน class diagram ของระบบช่วยตัดสินใจก่อนผ่าตัด ครูจะแตก User ด้วย generalisation เป็นผู้ดูแล ศัลยแพทย์ และวิสัญญีแพทย์ เพื่อให้แต่ละบทบาทมีความสัมพันธ์ของตัวเอง และใน use case ของ prep/import ที่เขียนให้ผู้ป่วยซิงก์ wearable กับแล็บส่งผลมารวมเป็น flow เดียว เธอให้กลับไปถามว่า “ฟังก์ชันนี้ใครเป็นคนทำ”

The deck’s own table fails its own test

She says the mobile-banking NFR table on the slide was generated as a sketch, then uses it as the counter-example: “อย่างรวดเร็ว” is not a requirement, because nothing in it can be checked. A row only becomes usable rewritten as Given / When / Then with seconds in it. The e-commerce payment wireframe on the later slides is a sketch for the same reason — she says the model usually does better. 1:49:02 1:38:31

ครูบอกว่าตาราง NFR ของ mobile banking บนสไลด์เป็นภาพร่างที่ให้โมเดลช่วยเจน แล้วใช้มันเป็นตัวอย่างผิด: “อย่างรวดเร็ว” ไม่ใช่ requirement เพราะตรวจอะไรไม่ได้ แต่ละแถวจะใช้ได้ก็ต่อเมื่อเขียนใหม่เป็น Given / When / Then ที่มีหน่วยวินาที ส่วน wireframe หน้าจ่ายเงินของอีคอมเมิร์ซก็เป็นภาพร่างด้วยเหตุผลเดียวกัน

Input design, from the postal code up

Instead of “validate the address”, she gives the recipe: ask for the postal code first, let the system narrow to amphoe and tambon, then let the user pick — which means the designer has to build the province → district → sub-district tables. And on a clinical summary screen, group the fields by the flow the doctor follows, so the screen produces understanding rather than a field list. 1:24:23 1:27:55

แทนที่จะบอกว่า “ตรวจสอบที่อยู่” ครูให้สูตรจริง: ให้กรอกรหัสไปรษณีย์ก่อน ระบบค่อยแคบลงเป็นอำเภอและตำบล แล้วให้ผู้ใช้เลือก — แปลว่าคนออกแบบต้องเตรียมตารางจังหวัด → อำเภอ → ตำบลไว้ และหน้าจอสรุปทางคลินิกควรจัดกลุ่มข้อมูลตาม flow ที่แพทย์ใช้ เพื่อให้เกิดความเข้าใจ ไม่ใช่เรียงเป็นรายการฟิลด์

8 · The cases she showed, and where NFRs come from

Still from the 19–20 Nov recordings. Watch the UI class at 1:12:25

A convenience-store POS, walked as an interface

Her real-world case for navigation and input: the touchscreen at a convenience store, with two roles — the salesperson at the till and the manager who opens the store in the morning — each with its own functions. The screen even carries the words to say, prompting the salesperson (“รับอันนี้เพิ่มไหม”), and it makes the till capture customer sex and age band on every basket, which she then justifies by repeat purchase, product-to-customer mapping and display arrangement. The deck has no case of this kind at all. 1:12:25

กรณีจริงที่ครูใช้สอน navigation และ input คือหน้าจอสัมผัสของร้านสะดวกซื้อ ซึ่งมีสองบทบาท — พนักงานขายที่เคาน์เตอร์กับผู้จัดการที่ต้องเปิดร้านตอนเช้า — แต่ละบทบาทมีฟังก์ชันของตัวเอง หน้าจอยังมีคำพูดให้พนักงานใช้ (“รับอันนี้เพิ่มไหม”) และบังคับให้เก็บเพศกับช่วงอายุของลูกค้าในทุกตะกร้า ซึ่งครูอธิบายว่ามีไว้จับการซื้อซ้ำ จับคู่สินค้ากับลูกค้า และจัดวางสินค้า

Organisational standards, and why the green bank changes colour

She has had bank UX teams in class: whatever the platform — mobile or web — a central design team owns the standard, so the apps look like the same organisation. The palette still moves: the green bank restyles its green so the mood does not read as dated, because each generation asks for different colour. Standards and personalisation sit together, and neither is on the slide. 1:05:28

ครูเคยเชิญทีม UX ของธนาคารมาคุยในคลาส: ไม่ว่าจะเป็นแอปบนมือถือหรือเว็บ ทีมออกแบบส่วนกลางเป็นเจ้าของมาตรฐาน ทำให้ทุกแอปดูเป็นองค์กรเดียวกัน แต่สีก็ยังขยับ — ธนาคารสีเขียวปรับเฉดเขียวเพื่อไม่ให้ดูล้าสมัย เพราะคนแต่ละรุ่นขอสีต่างกัน มาตรฐานกับการปรับให้เข้ากับคนใช้จึงอยู่ด้วยกัน

A form critiqued for missing units

On the slide's break-even-point calculator she calls the defect live: the title and the grouped fields are right, but every numeric field is missing its unit and none says in the field what to enter. It is the same rule as the six validation checks, applied by eye rather than listed. 39:45

บนสไลด์เครื่องคำนวณจุดคุ้มทุน ครูชี้ข้อบกพร่องสด ๆ: หัวข้อกับกลุ่มฟิลด์ถูกแล้ว แต่ทุกช่องตัวเลขไม่มีหน่วย และไม่มีคำใบ้ในช่องว่าต้องกรอกอะไร — เป็นกฎเดียวกับการตรวจข้อมูลเข้าหกข้อ แต่ใช้ด้วยสายตา ไม่ได้ไล่เป็นรายการ

Where NFRs come from in practice

Three sources she names that no deck lists. A developer-side quality goal: write once in Flutter and deploy to iOS and Android. A measurement discipline: teams stress-test a simulated production environment, which is why figures like 2,000 and 10,000 requests per second have to be measured rather than guessed. And a domain where safety NFRs must be hunted: one term project, Vital Lens, covers safety in a car-manufacturing plant. 16:42 1:35:28 2:13:33

แหล่งที่มาของ NFR สามทางที่ไม่มีในสไลด์: คุณภาพฝั่งนักพัฒนา — เขียนครั้งเดียวด้วย Flutter แล้ว deploy บน iOS กับ Android, วินัยการวัด — ทีมทดสอบ stress test ใน production environment ที่จำลองขึ้น จึงต้องวัดตัวเลขอย่าง 2,000 หรือ 10,000 request ต่อวินาที ไม่ใช่เดา, และโดเมนที่ต้องไล่หา safety NFR เอง — ตัวอย่างโครงงาน Vital Lens เรื่องความปลอดภัยในโรงงานผลิตรถยนต์

The system recommends, the doctor decides

A constraint she takes from a student's project and turns into a requirement pattern: what the system recommends is not enforced automatically; the doctor stays in the loop and can override or rewrite the recommended sentence. Stated as an NFR (human control), it becomes a functional requirement later — permissions, an edit screen, an audit trail. 19:11

ข้อจำกัดที่ครูหยิบจากโครงงานนิสิตมาเป็นรูปแบบของ requirement: สิ่งที่ระบบแนะนำไม่ได้ถูกบังคับใช้ทันที แพทย์ยังอยู่ในวงและสามารถ override หรือเขียนประโยคที่ระบบแนะนำใหม่ได้ เมื่อเขียนเป็น NFR (การควบคุมโดยมนุษย์) มันจะกลายเป็น functional requirement ตามมา — สิทธิ์การแก้ หน้าจอแก้ไข และ audit trail

Individual assignments

Homework, with model answers

Quiz 1 covers the fundamentals; Quiz 2 covers elicitation, analysis and negotiation; Quiz 3 is the modelling assignment on the Happy Fitness case; Quiz 4 is the individual assignment on PTSIMS; P7 and P8 are the two assignments set after the midterm. Read the guide, cover the answer, then write yours.

Quiz 1 — the ten questions

20 marks, 10 × 2, about 30 minutes. Read the guide, cover the answer, then write yours; the models are Thai with English terms.

Q1จงระบุความสำคัญของกระบวนการวิศวกรรมความต้องการ (กระบวนการนี้ทำเพื่ออะไร ได้ผลลัพธ์คืออะไร นำไปใช้ทำอะไร)

Use Lesson 1 · clause 5 and clause 7 · slides 38–60

Marker wants: purpose; the five activities; the three outputs; what those outputs feed.

กระบวนการ RE แปลงความต้องการของผู้มีส่วนได้ส่วนเสีย ระบบเดิม กฎหมาย และความรู้เฉพาะโดเมน ให้เป็นข้อกำหนดที่ตกลงร่วมกันและตรวจสอบได้ ประกอบด้วย 5 กิจกรรม: elicitation, analysis & negotiation, specification, validation และ management ผลลัพธ์มี 3 อย่าง: agreed requirements, เอกสารข้อกำหนด (StRS/SyRS/SRS) และ system model ผลลัพธ์นี้ใช้เป็น baseline ของ design, การประมาณเวลาและต้นทุน, การเขียน test case เพื่อ verification/validation และการควบคุมการเปลี่ยนแปลงด้วย traceability/impact analysis เพราะข้อผิดพลาดด้าน requirement เป็นจุดที่แก้แพงที่สุดเมื่อพบช้า (1–2 หน่วยที่ requirement เทียบกับ 200 ที่ maintenance)

Q2จงระบุความสำคัญของเอกสารข้อกำหนดความต้องการระบบ/ซอฟต์แวร์มา 2 รายการ

Use Lesson 1 · clause 12 · slides 65, 88–89

Marker wants: two distinct reasons with a consequence each — scope/agreement and verification/traceability.

1) ข้อตกลงและ scope baseline ที่ผูกพัน — ใช้ตัดสินว่า feature ใดอยู่ในขอบเขต ใช้ควบคุม scope creep และเป็นเครื่องมือสื่อสารกับผู้อ่านหลายกลุ่ม (client, PM, architect, QA, developer) ซึ่งแต่ละกลุ่มอ่านเพื่อคนละ purpose
2) ฐานของ verification & validation และ traceability — test case และ acceptance criteria อ้างอิงจากเอกสารนี้ และเมื่อ requirement เปลี่ยน ใช้ trace ย้อนกลับไปยัง need และไปข้างหน้าถึง design/test เพื่อประเมินผลกระทบ

Q3จงระบุเหตุผลว่าทำไมในองค์กรเดียวกัน ไม่จำเป็นต้องมี requirements engineering process แบบเดียวกัน

Use Lesson 1 · slides 112–113 · the four tailoring factors (technical, organisational, human, domain/business)

Marker wants: the four factor groups named, one example each, and the tailoring conclusion.

เพราะกระบวนการต้อง tailor ตามปัจจัย 4 กลุ่ม: technical (ชนิด ขนาด และความซับซ้อนของระบบ), organisational (วัฒนธรรม มาตรฐาน โครงสร้างและความเร็วในการอนุมัติ), human (ทักษะของทีม และความพร้อม/เวลาของผู้มีส่วนได้ส่วนเสีย) และ domain/business (โดเมนและกฎหมาย เช่น PDPA หรือ HIPAA) โครงการเล็กที่ requirement ชัดใช้กระบวนการเบาและ iterate เร็ว ส่วนระบบ safety-critical หรือระบบที่มี regulator ต้องมี review, validation และ traceability มากกว่า สไลด์ 113 สรุปว่าไม่มี RE process ในอุดมคติแบบเดียว

Q4จงยกตัวอย่างความต้องการระบบ/ซอฟต์แวร์ มา 2 รายการ ของระบบบันทึกสุขภาพอิเล็กทรอนิกส์ (EHR) โดยคำนึงถึงโครงสร้างของประโยค, language criteria และ requirements characteristic

Use Lesson 2 · clause 8, clause 9, clause 10, clause 11 · slides 24–35

Marker wants: two EHR requirements in the sentence pattern; a measurable condition; a named characteristic satisfied; no vague words.

1) The EHR system shall display the patient’s allergy list within 2 seconds of opening the patient record, for at least 95% of requests during clinic hours.
— หนึ่ง requirement, มี measurable condition (2 s, 95%, clinic hours), verifiable และเป็น capability ของระบบ ไม่ใช่ของผู้ใช้
2) The EHR system shall record an audit-log entry containing the user ID, patient ID, timestamp and action whenever a patient record is viewed.
— ตอบ constraint ของ PDPA/HIPAA, ตรวจสอบได้ และไม่ใช้คำกำกวม
ทั้งสองใช้โครงสร้าง [system] shall [function] [object] [condition/constraint] และแยกหนึ่ง requirement ต่อหนึ่งประโยค

Q5จงยกตัวอย่าง Concept of operation ของระบบใด ๆ มา 1 ระบบ

Use Lesson 1 · clause 14 · slides 99–102

Marker wants: organisation-level intent, one concrete system, and what ConOps deliberately leaves out.

ConOps คือมุมมองระดับองค์กร/ธุรกิจถึงความตั้งใจและสภาพการดำเนินงาน ก่อนตัดสินใจสร้างระบบ ตัวอย่างระบบนัดหมายผู้ป่วย: ปัจจุบันผู้ป่วยโทรนัดที่เคาน์เตอร์ อัตรา no-show ประมาณ 30% และการเตือนทำด้วยมือ องค์กรต้องการลด no-show ให้ผู้ป่วยจองหรือเลื่อนนัดเองได้ และให้เจ้าหน้าที่เห็นตารางนัดรายวัน ConOps จึงอธิบายปัญหา เป้าหมาย ผู้ใช้ และสภาพแวดล้อม โดยไม่ระบุสถาปัตยกรรมหรือฟังก์ชันซอฟต์แวร์

Q6จงยกตัวอย่าง System operational concept ของระบบที่ได้ตอบในข้อ 5

Use Lesson 1 · clause 14 · slides 102–106

Marker wants: system-level operation of the same system — actors, modes, assumptions, constraints.

OpsCon ของระบบเดียวกันมองจากฝั่งระบบว่าจะดำเนินงานอย่างไร: ผู้ป่วยจองและเลื่อนนัดผ่านแอป ระบบส่ง reminder 24 ชั่วโมงก่อนนัดทาง push และ fallback เป็น SMS เมื่อไม่มีการยืนยัน เจ้าหน้าที่เห็น dashboard ตารางนัด มี operational modes: normal, degraded (ส่งได้เฉพาะ SMS) และ failover (พิมพ์รายการนัดสำรอง) พร้อม assumptions เช่น ผู้ป่วยมีเบอร์โทรที่ใช้ได้ และ constraints เช่น PDPA, response 2 วินาที และ availability 99.9%

Q7จงระบุความต้องการของระบบ/ซอฟต์แวร์ใด ๆ มา 1 รายการ พร้อมระบุ requirements attributes และเนื้อหาของ attributes ของตัวอย่างนั้น

Use Lesson 2 · clause 14 · slides 39–44

Marker wants: one requirement and all eight attributes with values that fit it.

Requirement: The appointment system shall send a reminder to the patient 24 hours before the appointment.
Attributes: Identification REQ-APPT-014 (unique, never reused) · Priority Must (MoSCoW) · Dependency REQ-APPT-010 (contact data) · Risk Medium (SMS gateway availability) · Source patient focus group, 12 Oct 2026 · Rationale ลด no-show 30% · Difficulty Medium (ประมาณ 3 person-days) · Type Functional (system requirement)

Q8จงอธิบายวัตถุประสงค์และตัวอย่างการประยุกต์ใช้ Iterative และ Recursive approach เพื่อการระบุความต้องการซอฟต์แวร์

Use Lesson 2 · clause 16 · slides 46, 48

Marker wants: same-level repetition vs descent to a lower level, with one example each.

Iterative (ทำซ้ำ) ใช้กระบวนการเดิมซ้ำที่ระดับ abstraction เดิม เพื่อให้ requirement ครบและละเอียดขึ้นจาก feedback เช่น รอบแรกทำระบบนัดหมายผู้ป่วยนอก รอบถัดไปเพิ่มผู้ป่วยในและตารางแพทย์ โดยยังอยู่ที่ระดับระบบเดียวกัน
Recursive (เรียกซ้ำ) ใช้ชุดกระบวนการเดิมกับระดับที่ต่ำลงของ system element เช่น system → subsystem → software: จากระบบนัดหมาย → subsystem การจอง → module ตรวจสอบสิทธิ์ โดย requirement ไหลลงและ trace กลับได้
สรุป: ต่างกันที่ระดับ — ทำซ้ำระดับเดิม vs ลงลึกอีกระดับ

Q9ในการระบุความต้องการของผู้มีส่วนได้ส่วนเสียและความต้องการซอฟต์แวร์ เหตุใดจึงต้องทำความเข้าใจ External environment, Organization environment, Business operation และ System operation

Use Lesson 1 · clause 9 · slides 92, 96–97 (Figure 3)

Marker wants: four contexts, what each supplies, and why that protects the requirement.

External environment — กฎหมาย regulation ตลาด เทคโนโลยี และคู่แข่ง กำหนด constraint ที่ระบบต้องทำหรือห้ามทำ เช่น PDPA/HIPAA
Organization environment — นโยบาย มาตรฐาน และวัฒนธรรมองค์กร กำหนด standard และวิธีทำงานที่ requirement ต้องสอดคล้อง
Business operation — กระบวนการธุรกิจ กติกา และโหมดการทำงาน ทำให้ requirement สะท้อนงานจริงและพบ stakeholder/use case ครบ
System operation — การทำงานของระบบในสภาพจริงและโหมดต่าง ๆ กำหนดขอบเขต system/software และ operational scenario
เหตุผลรวม: requirement ต้อง trace กลับขึ้นไปถึง business และ stakeholder need (Figure 3) ถ้าไม่เข้าใจบริบทจะได้ requirement ที่ขัดกฎ ขัด business rule หรือแยกขอบเขตผิด

Q10ให้ระบุปัญหาของกระบวนการวิศวกรรมความต้องการ และแนวทางในการแก้ไขมา 2 รายการ

Use Lesson 1 · clause 11 · slides 78–80

Marker wants: two named problems, a cause, and a specific remedy each.

1) Requirement กำกวมและผู้ใช้ไม่บอกสิ่งที่ทำเป็นกิจวัตร (unspoken requirements) — แนวทาง: shared glossary, template/ประโยคมาตรฐาน, job shadowing และ observation, prototype/wireframe เพื่อให้ผู้ใช้เห็นภาพ
2) Gold plating และ scope creep (ขอเกินจำเป็นและเพิ่มเรื่อย ๆ) — แนวทาง: จัดลำดับด้วย MoSCoW และตรวจกับ business KPI, กำหนด scope baseline และใช้ change control (CCB) เพื่อเลื่อนสิ่งที่ไม่จำเป็นไป phase ถัดไป

Quiz 2 — the five questions

Individual Assignment #2, 20 marks (6/2/4/4/4). The paper asks about your own term project; the models below use a hospital appointment system, so substitute your system.

Q1[6 คะแนน] จากโจทย์ term project ระบุ requirements sources, requirements gathering method และสิ่งที่คาดหวังว่าจะได้ พร้อมตัวอย่างผลลัพธ์ 2 sources

Use Lesson 3 · clause 4, clause 8, clause 10, clause 11, clause 12

Marker wants: two sources; for each, the method, what you expect from it, and one concrete output — not a list of techniques.

Source 1 — ผู้ป่วยนอกและเจ้าหน้าที่ลงทะเบียน. Method: interview ผู้ป่วย 5 คนและเจ้าหน้าที่ 2 คน แล้วตามด้วย questionnaire กับผู้ป่วย 100 คนเพื่อวัดความถี่ของปัญหา. คาดหวัง: ความต้องการและ pain point ที่แท้จริง พร้อมลำดับความสำคัญ. ตัวอย่างผลลัพธ์: “ผู้ป่วยต้องการเลื่อนนัดเองโดยไม่ต้องโทร” และ “เจ้าหน้าที่ต้องการเห็นตารางนัดรายวันพร้อมช่องว่าง”
Source 2 — เอกสารเดิมของคลินิก. Method: document analysis ของสมุดนัด ใบลงทะเบียน และประกาศนโยบายการนัด. คาดหวัง: ฟิลด์ข้อมูล กฎธุรกิจ และข้อยกเว้นที่ระบบใหม่ต้องรองรับ. ตัวอย่างผลลัพธ์: ฟิลด์ HN คลินิก แพทย์ วันที่ เวลา; กฎ “นัดซ้ำได้ไม่เกิน 30 วัน”; ข้อยกเว้น “แพทย์ลา/วันหยุดนักขัตฤกษ์”
Source 3 (ถ้าต้องการเพิ่มความครบ) — observation. เฝ้าดูเช้าคลินิกหนึ่งวันเพื่อจับ workaround; ผลลัพธ์: “เจ้าหน้าที่จดนัดซ้ำในสมุดแยกอีกเล่ม” ซึ่งเป็น requirement ที่ไม่มีใครบอก

Q2[2 คะแนน] term project ใช้ analysis approach (BPA, BPI, BPR) แบบใด ด้วยเหตุผลใด

Use Lesson 4 · clause 16

Marker wants: one named approach and reasons tied to change, risk and efficiency — not a definition of all three.

เลือก BPI. กระบวนการนัดมีอยู่แล้วแต่ยังไม่มีประสิทธิภาพ: จองทางโทรศัพท์เท่านั้น ไม่มี reminder และเจ้าหน้าที่คีย์ซ้ำ. BPI เปลี่ยนแปลงปานกลาง เสี่ยงต่ำ–ปานกลาง และปรับ efficiency ของ as-is ได้โดยไม่รื้อทั้งกระบวนการ. BPA จะ automate งานเดิมและคงคอขวดไว้ ส่วน BPR เป็นการรื้อกระบวนการทั้งหมด เสี่ยงและต้นทุนสูงเกินไปสำหรับโรงพยาบาลและกรอบเวลาโครงงาน

Q3[4 คะแนน] ใช้ analysis strategy ใด ด้วยเหตุผลใด ระบุมา 2 รายการ

Use Lesson 4 · clause 17. The paper also names activity elimination; the deck teaches seven strategies and does not separate it.

Marker wants: two named strategies, why each fits your problem, and the result each would produce. If you use activity elimination, say which activity adds no value.

1) Root-cause analysis — no-show. ให้ผู้ใช้ระบุปัญหาที่จัดลำดับแล้วและสาเหตุที่เป็นไปได้ทั้งหมด (ลืม, เดินทางลำบาก, รอคิวนาน) แล้ว analyst หา solution และสาเหตุร่วม. ผลลัพธ์: reminder 24 ชั่วโมง, การเลื่อนนัดออนไลน์, และการจัดคิวให้ตรงเวลา ซึ่งแก้ได้หลายอาการจากสาเหตุเดียว.
2) Duration analysis — เวลาตรวจ. วัดเวลาแต่ละขั้นเทียบเวลารวม (ผู้ป่วยใช้เวลา 90 นาที แต่พบแพทย์จริง 20 นาที) แล้วรวมขั้นที่ทำแยกกันได้ให้ขนาน. ผลลัพธ์: รวมลงทะเบียนกับ triage และทำ lab/จ่ายยาแบบคู่ขนาน.
Activity elimination (ถ้าเลือก). ถ้ากิจกรรมไม่สร้างคุณค่า เช่น การคีย์ข้อมูลซ้ำสองระบบ ให้ตัดกิจกรรมนั้นทิ้ง ไม่ใช่เอาเทคโนโลยีไป automate มัน — นี่คือความต่างจาก BPA

Q4[4 คะแนน] ในขั้น requirements analysis เหตุใดจึงต้องทำ system modeling และ requirements allocation to each part of system architecture

Use Lesson 4 · clause 10 and clause 12

Marker wants: a purpose for modelling, a purpose for allocation, and a consequence of each — not two definitions.

System modeling. แบบจำลอง as-is และ to-be ทำให้ assumption มองเห็น ตรวจความครบและความสอดคล้อง (missing/conflicting requirements) และใช้สื่อสารกับผู้มีส่วนได้ส่วนเสีย. ถ้าไม่ทำ จะ 발견ข้อขัดแย้งช้าและ SRS จะไม่ครบ.
Requirements allocation. จับแต่ละ requirement ลง component ที่รับผิดชอบ เพื่อพิสูจน์ coverage (ทุกข้อมีเจ้าภาพ) ค้นพบ interface requirement ที่ไม่มีใครบอก และรองรับ impact analysis เมื่อ component เปลี่ยน. Allocation ยังเป็นฐานของการประมาณงานและออกแบบสถาปัตยกรรม เพราะทำให้เห็นว่า requirement ใดกระทบหลายส่วน (global scope)

Q5[4 คะแนน] เมื่อ requirement ขัดแย้งกันหรือผู้เกี่ยวข้องให้ความสำคัญต่างกัน จะแก้ไขอย่างเป็นขั้นตอนอย่างไร พร้อมเป้าหมาย สมมุติฐาน ผู้ที่เกี่ยวข้อง และผลลัพธ์

Use Lesson 4 · clause 14 and clause 15

Marker wants: four ordered steps, plus goal, assumptions, stakeholders and expected outputs — the paper lists all five fields.

เป้าหมาย: ได้ข้อตกลงที่อธิบายได้และบันทึกไว้ พร้อมข้อกำหนดที่อัปเดตแล้ว.
สมมุติฐาน: stakeholder ที่เกี่ยวข้องเข้าร่วมได้; มีผู้มีอำนาจตัดสิน; ตกลงเกณฑ์การตัดสินก่อนให้คะแนน.
ผู้ที่เกี่ยวข้อง: เจ้าของธุรกิจ/สปอนเซอร์, ผู้ใช้ปลายทาง, IT/architect, project manager และ facilitator ที่เป็นกลาง.
ผลลัพธ์ที่คาดหวัง: decision record (ข้อความ เหตุผล ผู้ตัดสิน วันที่), prioritized requirements ที่อัปเดต, action items และ traceability ที่อัปเดต.
วิธีการดำเนินการ:
1. บันทึกความขัดแย้งหรือความเห็นต่างเป็นรายข้อ (requirement ID, แหล่งที่มา, ผลกระทบ) และตรวจว่าข้อมูลครบ
2. ตกลงเกณฑ์และให้คะแนนด้วยหลักฐาน (value vs penalty, MoSCoW, cost/benefit)
3. ประชุมเจรจาแบบ information → discussion → resolution โดยมีประธานที่ไม่ใช่ stakeholder และเสนอทางเลือก/trade-off
4. บันทึกข้อตกลงและสิ่งที่แต่ละฝ่ายเสียสละ อัปเดต requirement/RTM และสื่อสารการตัดสินใจ

Quiz 3 — Happy Fitness modelling assignment

The paper says 25 points and its questions sum to 35 (the activity-diagram item carries no mark), so read the mark on each question, not the header. Six modelling tasks on one case.

Q1Create a use case diagram for the PTSIMS.

10 marks · Lesson 5

Marker wants: the boundary and its name; two external systems as actors; use cases as verb phrases; one include and one extend with the arrow pointing the right way.

Actors outside the boundary: Customer/Member (primary business), PT Assistant Manager and Personal Trainer (primary system), Credit card company (external server), Email system (external server). Use cases inside: Apply for membership, Purchase training programme, Pay by credit card, Reserve a session, Reschedule a session, Record a training session, Produce the monthly report, Export the payment file, Notify three sessions remaining. Relationships: Pay by credit card includes Verify payment (always required); Reschedule extends Reserve (optional, only when the member changes the slot); Apply online and Apply at the counter may generalise Apply for membership. One boundary, a name above it, and no use case without an actor.

Q2Create a use case description for payment by credit card (items 4 and 5).

5 marks · Lesson 5

Marker wants: all eight fields; a four-part normal flow in SVDPI; alternate and exceptional kept distinct.

Eight fields: name “Pay by credit card” · ID UC-PAY-01 · type detail, essential · primary actor Member · brief charge the selected programme and issue a receipt · importance high · stakeholders member, PT-AM, credit card company, finance · trigger external: member chooses to pay. Normal flow in SVDPI, four parts: the member selects a programme; the system validates the card details; the system requests verification from the credit card company and changes the programme status to paid; the system sends the receipt to the member. Alternate: the card is invalid — the system tells the member and offers cancel or another card. Exceptional: the credit card company does not respond — the system records the transaction as pending and tells the member it will retry.

Q3Create an activity diagram for the payment use case.

No mark stated · Lesson 5

Marker wants: three lanes including the company; a decision with written guards; a fork with a matching join.

Three lanes: Member (top), System, Credit card company. Initial node in Member → “enter card details” → system “validate format” → decision “details complete?” with [yes]/[no]; [no] returns to entry. On [yes] → “send verification request” in the company lane → decision “valid?” — [yes] → fork: “issue receipt” and “update programme status”, then join → final-activity node; [no] → “show invalid message” → decision “cancel or retry?”; retry loops back to entry, cancel ends at a final-flow node. Every fork has a join, every guard is written, and the object node “payment record” flows between System and the company.

Q4Draw a class diagram for the problem-domain classes.

10 marks · Lesson 6

Marker wants: domain classes only; attributes kept apart from operations; multiplicity at both ends; one composition named as such.

Classes: Member (memberID, name, dateOfBirth, address, email, emergencyContact), Membership, PersonalTrainer (ptID, name, expertise), TrainingProgramme (programmeID, sessions: 10|30|50, preference, status), BoughtPackage, Reservation (date, time, status), TrainingSession (date, time, sessionsUsed), Payment (amount, status), CreditCard (holder, number, expiry, country). Relationships: Member 1 — * BoughtPackage; BoughtPackage 1 — * Reservation; Reservation 1 — * TrainingSession; BoughtPackage 1 — * Payment; Payment 1 — 1 CreditCard (composition — the card record exists for that payment); PersonalTrainer 1 — * TrainingSession. PT-AM manages PersonalTrainer. Attributes carry no getters/setters; visibility marks on at least one class.

Q5Draw a sequence diagram from the payment use case description.

5 marks · after the midterm

Marker wants: lifelines in time order; messages in order; one alt fragment with both branches.

Lifelines left to right: Member, :PaymentUI (boundary), :PaymentController (control), :CreditCardCompany (external), :EmailSystem. Messages in time order: enterCardDetails() → validate() → verifyPayment() → success → createReceipt() → sendEmail(); on failure → showInvalidMessage(). Use an alt fragment with [valid] and [invalid] branches, and a dashed return arrow for each call. Sequence diagrams are Lesson 7 material — not on this page and not on the midterm.

Q6Create a behavioural state machine diagram for a bought package.

5 marks · after the midterm

Marker wants: named states; event and guard on every transition; the three-sessions state drawn as a state, not a note.

States: Purchased → Active (first session recorded) → ThreeSessionsRemaining (notification sent) → Completed (all sessions used). Transitions carry events and guards: recordSession [sessionsLeft > 3], recordSession [sessionsLeft = 3] / notify member, recordSession [sessionsLeft = 0] / status = Completed. A cancel transition from Purchased or Active to Cancelled if refunds are allowed. State machine diagrams are Lesson 7 material — after the midterm.

Q1Applying the technique for defining two non-functional requirements, explain how they affect the system or the system architecture. (5 points)เลือก NFR สองข้อโดยใช้เทคนิคที่เรียน แล้วอธิบายว่ามันกระทบระบบหรือสถาปัตยกรรมอย่างไร

เทคนิคคือ goal decomposition จากเป้าหมายธุรกิจ (Lesson 8 clause 6) แล้วทำให้วัดได้ด้วย quality attribute scenario (clause 9) เขียนสองข้อนี้ (1) Availability: source = สมาชิกและ PT, stimulus = เปิดตารางจองหรือบันทึก session, environment = เวลาทำการ จ.–ส. 06:00–22:00, artifact = ระบบ PTSIMS, response = ระบบให้บริการต่อโดยไม่ต้องให้ผู้ใช้ลองใหม่, measure = พร้อมใช้งาน 99.5% ต่อเดือน (วัดด้วย external uptime monitor), กู้คืนภายใน 30 นาทีเมื่อ node หนึ่งล้ม (RTO ≤ 30 นาที) และเสียข้อมูลไม่เกิน 5 นาที (RPO ≤ 5 นาที ด้วย continuous replication + backup รายวัน) (2) Security: source = ผู้ใช้ทั่วไปบนอินเทอร์เน็ต, stimulus = ส่งข้อมูลบัตรเพื่อซื้อโปรแกรม, environment = การชำระเงินผ่านหน้าเว็บ, artifact = โมดูลชำระเงิน, response = ข้อมูลบัตรไม่ถูกเก็บในฐานข้อมูลของเราและการสื่อสารทุกเส้นเข้ารหัส, measure = TLS 1.2 ขึ้นไปทุกเส้น, เข้ารหัส at rest ด้วย AES-256, ไม่มี PAN ในฐานข้อมูล (เก็บเฉพาะ token, last 4 หลัก และ transaction ID), จำกัดสิทธิ์ตาม role — PT-AM จัดการข้อมูล PT และออกรายงาน ส่วน PT อัปเดต session ของตัวเอง — และ penetration test ก่อน go-live ต้องไม่มี finding ระดับ critical/high ผลต่อสถาปัตยกรรม: availability บังคับให้มี load balancer กับ application server สองตัว และฐานข้อมูลแบบ primary + standby ที่ promote ได้; security บังคับให้มี firewall/WAF ที่ขอบเครือข่าย, วาง database ใน private subnet ที่ไม่มี public IP, ให้ gateway ของบริษัทบัตรอยู่นอกขอบเขต ระบบเราเห็นแค่ผลอนุมัติ ไม่เห็นเลขบัตร, ส่งอีเมลด้วย SMTP over TLS และส่งไฟล์เงินเดือนด้วย SFTP ไม่ใช่อีเมล — ทั้งสองข้อนี้คือสิ่งที่ต้องเห็นใน deployment diagram ของข้อ 2. ในคำตอบจริงควรผูก NFR กับเลข requirement ของโจทย์ด้วย: security ครอบข้อ 1, 2, 4 และ 5; availability ครอบข้อ 6 และ 7
