It improves efficiency without the very high risk of reengineering. If the hospital's strategy is to remove walk-in booking entirely and lead with telemedicine, that is BPR, and it must be justified by the risk the organisation can carry, not by novelty.

Q16Name the seven analysis strategies, choose one for three scenarios, and name the four common analysis mistakes.

Marker wants: seven named strategies; three justified choices; four mistakes with their consequence.

The seven: problem analysis, root-cause analysis, duration analysis, activity-based costing, informal benchmarking, outcome analysis and technology analysis.
Scenarios. Frequent stock-outs: root-cause analysis — users list prioritised problems and all possible causes; the analyst finds common causes. A clinic visit that takes 90 minutes but only 20 minutes of clinical work: duration analysis — compare step time with total time and integrate or parallelise. An insurance claim that ends with the customer arranging their own repair: outcome analysis — start from the desired outcome (a repaired car) and extend the process to contract an authorised repair shop.
Four mistakes: reducing analysis time (builds the wrong product), requirements gold plating (scope creep, missed deadline and budget), developer gold plating (unrequested technical features), and lack of user involvement (a technically working system that users reject). Each trades a small saving now for a large cost later.

Lesson 5

Fourteen questions. Use cases, descriptions and activity diagrams.

Q1Name the three representations of the functional model and say what question each answers.

Marker wants: three named views; the question each answers; the logical/implementation-independent point.

Use case diagram — what functionality the system offers, to which actors, inside which boundary (scope).
Use case description — for one use case, how it unfolds: trigger, actors, normal and alternate flows (detail).
Activity diagram — the business process across activities and roles: decisions, parallel work, who does what (sequence). All three are logical: they do not commit to manual or computerised implementation.

Q2List the five elements of a use case diagram and explain where the boundary goes.

Marker wants: five elements; actors outside, use cases inside; the system name on the boundary.

Actors and actor relationships; use cases and use case relationships; the interaction (association) between actor and use case; the system boundary; the system name. Actors sit outside the boundary because they are external to the system; use cases sit inside it; the system name labels the boundary. The boundary is a scope decision: the SMS gateway is an actor, sending the message is a use case.

Q3How do you find actors, what kinds exist, and what are the four actor types?

Marker wants: the finding questions; five kinds; four types with one example each.

Ask who or what produces or consumes the system's data: who uses the main functions, who needs support, who maintains it, which devices it handles, which systems it interacts with, who cares about the result. Kinds: human, machine, external system, organisational unit, sensor. Types: primary business (benefits — employee paid), primary system (initiates — teller enters a deposit), external server (responds — credit bureau authorises), external receiver (gets value — warehouse receives a packing slip).

Q4Explain association multiplicity and actor generalisation, and correct the common misreading of the arrowhead.

Marker wants: no arrowhead = two-way, solid = one-way; generalisation = substitution; arrow ≠ initiation.

Multiplicity is the number of associations. No arrowhead means information flows both ways; a solid arrowhead means one way. The arrow shows the direction of information, not who initiates the use case — initiation is recorded by the primary actor in the description. Actor generalisation means instances of the specialised actor may substitute for the general one, inheriting its associations (a nurse can do what a staff member can do).

Q5Give the six-step procedure for creating a use case diagram and explain “right size”.

Marker wants: six ordered steps including the review/split-combine step; one sizing example.

1) Review the requirements definition. 2) Identify the boundary, primary actors and their goals, business processes and major use cases. 3) Carefully review the set — split or combine to the right size, and add missing cases. 4) Place and draw the use cases and actors. 5) Draw the subject boundary. 6) Add the associations. “Right size” means each ellipse is one goal a user can complete in one sitting (sea level): “Manage appointment” is too coarse; “Book”, “Reschedule”, “Cancel” are the right size, with “Remind patient” separate.

Q6Distinguish include, extend and generalisation, giving the arrow direction for each.

Marker wants: required vs optional; arrow from dependent to dependency; one example each; direction.

Include — the base incorporates the included behaviour as a required part; dashed arrow from base to the included case (both “Update grade” and “Generate Grade Report” include “Verify student ID”). Extend — the base is complete on its own; the extension adds optional behaviour; dashed arrow from the extension to the base (“Apply discount” extends “Checkout”). Generalisation — the specialised case inherits actors, behaviour and meaning; solid line with a hollow triangle pointing to the general case (“Phone order” and “Internet order” generalise “Place order”).

Q7Describe Cockburn's use case levels and say which one is the default for a use case.

Marker wants: three bands; five names; one example per band; sea level as default.

Summary: cloud (enterprise — sell goods, manage inventory) and kite (department — register students). User goal: sea level, one activity of about 2–20 minutes (book an appointment); this is the default. Subfunction: fish (log in, choose a class) and clam (validate login, insert an order line). Writing a sea-level goal with clam-level steps mixes levels and loses marks.

Q8List the fields of a use case description and write a short example for “Book appointment”.

Marker wants: eight fields; a filled example; the ID's traceability purpose.

Name (verb–noun), ID, type (overview/detail; essential/real), primary actor, brief description, importance, stakeholders, triggers (external or temporal), plus relationships and flows. Example: UC-APPT-03 · Book appointment; ID traces to REQ-APPT-014; type detail, essential; primary actor Patient; stakeholders patient, receptionist, manager; importance high (first release); trigger external — the patient requests a slot; brief — reserve a slot with a doctor and confirm it.

Q9Explain the three kinds of flow in a use case description, with one example of each.

Marker wants: three kinds; alternate and exceptional as the two cases of the third; concrete example.

The deck names three kinds; alternate and exceptional are the two cases of the third.
Normal flow — the usual activities: patient chooses a slot, system reserves it, system confirms.
Sub-flow — a decomposed normal step kept separate for clarity (e.g. “verify insurance” used inside booking).
Alternate or exceptional flow — alternate is a legitimate different path: the slot was taken while the patient decided, so the system offers the next three. Exceptional is a failure or blocked condition: the scheduling service is down, so the request is recorded for callback. Alternate is not a failure; exceptional is.

Q10Distinguish essential from real use cases, and overview from detail ones.

Marker wants: two independent axes; the Google Calendar example; why essential is preferred at requirements time.

Essential describes only implementation-independent issues; real commits to technology, design and UI. Overview documents only the overview and relationships; detail documents all parts, including the flow based on the activity diagram. They are independent: a real overview and an essential detail both exist. Example: essential — “receptionist matches the desired appointment time with the available time”; real — “receptionist looks up available dates on Google Calendar”. Essential is preferred at requirements time because a technology choice is a design decision that has not been negotiated.

Q11State the rules for writing the normal flow, then rewrite: “Appointment is booked.”

Marker wants: SVDPI; observer perspective; four parts; a rewritten step with subject and receiver.

Each step is subject–verb–direct object, optionally preposition–indirect object (SVDPI); the initiator and receiver are explicit; it is written from an independent observer's perspective; the set has four parts — the primary actor requests, the system validates, the system processes and may change state, the system returns the result; steps are about equal size and follow KISS. Rewrite: “The patient selects a time slot; the system reserves the slot and returns a confirmation to the patient.”

Q12Describe the process for creating use case descriptions.

Marker wants: priority first; overview/relationships; normal flow; alternate flows; user review; include/extend; repeat.

Choose a high-priority use case and write its overview and relationships parts; describe the normal flow in SVDPI steps; identify and write alternate and exceptional flows; review the description with the user to confirm it is correct; look for include, extend and generalisation opportunities and add or merge cases; repeat until the major use cases are documented. The review is a step: that is where missing actors and alternate flows are found.

Q13What is an activity diagram for, and what do the decision, merge, fork and join symbols mean?

Marker wants: process view across activities; decision vs merge; fork/join pairing; final node.

An activity diagram models a business process: the sequence of activities, the objects flowing between them, and the parties responsible. It can cover a workflow across several use cases, one use case, or one method. Decision (diamond) asks a guarded question and chooses one path; merge (diamond) rejoins alternatives; fork (bar) splits into parallel paths; join (bar) waits for all of them — never a fork without a join. A filled circle starts, a bullseye ends, and swimlanes assign activities to roles.

Q14How do you create a swimlane activity diagram, and what layout rules does the deck give?

Marker wants: the procedure; object flows; decision/parallelism; minimise crossings; left-to-right/top-to-bottom.

Choose the business process to set the scope; review the requirements definition, the use case diagram and the documentation collected; identify the activities and connect them with control flows, object flows and nodes; identify the decisions and the potential parallelism; draw the diagram. Add each activity's input and output as an object flow, put the most important individual or object at the top or left, minimise crossing lines, and lay it out left-to-right and/or top-to-bottom. In the appointment example: patient, reception and doctor lanes, a decision for a free slot whose paths merge before booking, then a final node — and a fork/join if confirmation and the calendar update run in parallel.

Lesson 6

8 questions

Q1Describe the four approaches for identifying objects and classes, and say which one a use-case description invites.

Marker wants: the named parts, not prose.

Textual analysis, brainstorming, common object list, patterns. A use-case description invites textual analysis: nouns become classes or attributes, verbs operations.

Q2For “Appointment”, classify each member as attribute or operation: startTime, reschedule(), status, validateSlot().

Marker wants: the named parts, not prose.

startTime and status are attributes (state); reschedule() and validateSlot() are operations (behaviour). A verb that acts is never an attribute.

Q3Read the multiplicities: Patient 1 — * Appointment, Doctor 1 — * Appointment. What does each end mean?

Marker wants: the named parts, not prose.

One patient has many appointments; each appointment belongs to exactly one patient. Same for doctor. Multiplicity is read at the end nearest the class it counts.

Q4Decide aggregation or composition, with a reason: Ward–Bed, Appointment–Slot.

Marker wants: the named parts, not prose.

Ward–Bed is aggregation: a bed survives the ward closing and can be reassigned. Appointment–Slot is composition: the slot exists for that appointment and is destroyed when it is cancelled.

Q5Why is Person abstract while Doctor is concrete? Give one consequence for a class diagram.

Marker wants: the named parts, not prose.

Person is never instantiated on its own; Doctor and Patient are. The diagram may show Person as a general class with the hollow triangle, and must not show objects of Person.

Q6Apply textual analysis to: “The clinic assigns a doctor to each appointment.” Name the classes, the operation and what the sentence says about multiplicity.

Marker wants: the named parts, not prose.

Classes: Clinic, Doctor, Appointment. Operation: assigns. “Each appointment” gives one doctor to many appointments — multiplicity 1..* at the Appointment end.

Q7List the seven steps and the three checks that follow them.

Marker wants: the named parts, not prose.

(1) textual analysis on descriptions; (2) use SVDPI flow sentences; (3) classes; (4) attributes; (5) operations; (6) relationships with collaborators; (7) visibility and multiplicity. Then (8) review and remove what is unnecessary; (9) incorporate patterns; (10) validate against the use-case diagrams and descriptions.

Q8The description says “the system sends the patient a reminder”, but the class diagram has no Reminder class or link. What is wrong, and which step catches it?

Marker wants: the named parts, not prose.

The structural model is incomplete: the object implied by the description is missing. Step 10 — review and validate, keeping use-case diagrams, descriptions and the class diagram consistent — is the check.

Lesson 7

8 questions. Sequence diagrams, state machines, and the check between them.

Q1Draw, or write out in order, the instance sequence diagram for “cancel an appointment”: name every participant, and give five messages with the right arrow type.

Marker wants: objects not classes; one scenario; sync vs async chosen and justified; order top to bottom; the slot released in the same scenario.

Participants: aPatient, :AppointmentUI, :Appointment, :SlotList, :Notification. Messages in order: (1) cancelRequest(apptID), synchronous, patient → UI (the patient waits for confirmation); (2) lookup(apptID), synchronous, UI → Appointment; (3) updateStatus(Cancelled), synchronous, UI → Appointment, guarded [status = Booked]; (4) releaseSlot(slot), synchronous, Appointment → SlotList — without it the slot is lost; (5) sendConfirmation(), asynchronous, UI → Notification, because the receipt does not block the cancellation. Activation bars on UI and Appointment for the duration of their handling; the lookup return can be omitted (obvious), the confirmation ID kept (not obvious).

Q2A classmate's diagram has: a solid arrow labelled return, no activation bars, a lifeline labelled Appointment, a destroy drawn as a dashed return, and an alt with no guards. Name each fault and the fix.

Marker wants: fault → fix pairs, all five, with the rule behind each.

(1) Return must be dashed, with an open arrowhead. (2) Every object that is doing work carries an activation bar; without it the reader cannot see who is busy. (3) A bare Appointment is a class — write :Appointment or aAppt : Appointment; at least a name or a type must be present. (4) Destroy is an × at the end of a lifeline (optionally <<destroy>>), not a return; the lifeline stops there. (5) Each subfragment of an alt starts with its own guard in square brackets, and the guards must be mutually exclusive.

Q3Choose the fragment for each: (a) send the reminder, retrying up to three times; (b) if the patient is outside the catchment, send a referral instead; (c) run three lab tests at the same time.

Marker wants: the fragment named, its guard written, and the distinction between alt and opt stated.

(a) loop [attempt ≤ 3 and not delivered] — one subfragment, repeated while its guard holds. (b) alt [outside catchment] / [inside catchment] if the diagram then continues differently; opt [outside catchment] if the referral is only an extra and the remaining flow is unchanged — that is the single-alternative case the deck defines. (c) par around the three requests, which then join; the tests are concurrent, not alternative. In all three the fragment rectangle spans the lifelines of the objects involved, and each subfragment carries its own guard.

Q4List the six steps for building a sequence diagram, and state two style rules that are marked in the drawing itself.

Marker wants: ordered steps; rules about order and naming, not vague style advice.

Steps: (1) set the context — the use case or one scenario; (2) identify the actors and objects; (3) draw a lifeline for each; (4) add messages left to right and top to bottom, with guards and parameters, omitting obvious returns; (5) add the activation bar to each object's lifeline; (6) validate — every step of the use-case description must appear as a message. Style rules that are marked: the initiator sits on the left; an actor and the object representing the same idea carry the same name; several objects of one class are named individually (aDailyReport : Report); returns are omitted when obvious.

Q5Give the states of an Appointment object in a clinic system, with the event that moves it into each state.

Marker wants: states (nouns) separate from events (operations); no black hole; each transition tied to an operation.

States: Booked (after book()), Rescheduled (after reschedule() with a new slot), Attended (after attend() at check-in), NoShow (after markNoShow() when the slot passes), Cancelled (after cancel() [!attended]), Archived (after archive() once the note is signed). Every state except Archived has at least one exit; Archived is the only one with no out-transition — and no state is a miracle: each has an incoming arrow. Reschedule is modelled as a state, or as a self-transition on Booked if the system overwrites the slot — either is acceptable if the behaviour is stated.

Q6Write three transition labels for a pharmacy dispensing order in the form event [guard] / action.

Marker wants: the three parts in the right order; guards mutually exclusive; actions that are operations of the object.

Examples: submit() [payment verified] / setStatus(Packed); dispense() [stock available] / setStatus(Ready); collect() [ID checked] / setStatus(Collected). The event is the operation that triggers the move; the guard is the condition that must hold, and no two guards out of one state may be true together; the action is an operation on the object, not a description (“pack the box” is not a label).

Q7A machine has Cancelled with no out-transition and Attended with no in-transition. Name each defect and repair it.

Marker wants: the two named defects; a repair that keeps the lifecycle consistent with the other models.

Cancelled is a black hole — the object can enter and never leave, so the state grows without an exit. Repair with archive() [retention expired] to the final state, or make it terminal on purpose by acknowledging it as the end of the object's life. Attended is a miracle — it is reachable by nothing, so it can never occur. Repair by adding the transition that the sequence diagram already implies: attend() [slot passed] from Booked. A machine with either defect contradicts the use-case description even if each arrow is drawn correctly.

Q8The order machine has Processing → Denied, but the sequence diagram has no message for it. What must be added, where, and why is a “read” message not enough?

Marker wants: the message named with C/U/D classification; its place on both diagrams; the reason a read cannot change state.

Add an Update message updateOrderStatus(Denied) on the sequence diagram, after the credit-card-clearance response and before the customer edit or withdrawal; the same operation must exist on the class diagram as an operation of Order. A read only copies state to the caller — it changes no attribute value, so no transition can be caused by it. The deck's rule is exact: every transition must correspond to a Create, Update or Delete message; then check that the actors match between the use case, the sequence diagram and the state machine, and that the message order matches the scenario.

Lesson 8

8 questions. Classifying, measuring, deriving, and trading off non-functional requirements.

Q1Classify each as functional or non-functional, and name the NFR class where it applies. (a) The system shall let a receptionist book an appointment. (b) The system shall keep the audit trail for five years. (c) The system shall encrypt patient data at rest and in transit. (d) The system shall send a reminder 24 hours before the appointment. (e) Any screen shall render within 2 seconds on the hospital network.

Marker wants: five correct labels, the class named for each NFR, and one sentence of reasoning per answer.

(a) Functional — a service the system provides. (b) Non-functional, external or product depending on the source: if it comes from a retention law it is external; if the hospital sets it, it is a product security requirement. Say which source you are assuming. (c) Non-functional, product — integrity and security, measurable as an encryption standard. (d) Functional — the system performs an action; the timing could be turned into an NFR (“delivered at least 24 hours before the slot, to 99% of patients with a phone number”). (e) Non-functional, product — performance, with a stated load. The test for the borderline ones: does the sentence name a service the system performs, or a property of how well it performs?

Q2Sort into product, process or external: (a) all clinical models shall be produced in the hospital's licensed modelling tool; (b) the system shall support 200 concurrent users on the ward network; (c) the system shall exchange lab results using HL7 FHIR; (d) the requirements document shall follow ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148; (e) the system shall be available 99.8% during clinic hours; (f) the system shall obtain consent before collecting personal data, as PDPA requires. Then name one item that can defensibly sit in two classes.

Marker wants: six labels; the “who is constrained” test stated; one overlap argued rather than asserted.

(a) Process — constrains the team's tools. (b) Product — capacity and performance of the system. (c) External — interoperability with other systems, driven by a standard outside the project. (d) Process — the development standard. (e) Product — reliability and availability. (f) External — a legal rule of the environment. The test is “who is constrained”: the system's behaviour is product, the team's way of working is process, the world the system must fit is external. Overlap: (c) is external in origin and simultaneously a product interface requirement — the deck says on slide 18 that a requirement can easily be classified under more than one heading, so name the origin and the effect rather than forcing one label.

Q3Rewrite each so it is objective and testable: (a) the system shall be user-friendly; (b) the system shall be highly available; (c) the system shall be secure; (d) the system shall respond quickly; (e) the system shall be scalable.

Marker wants: a number, a unit, a condition and a test for each; no adjective left standing alone.

(a) A nurse with no prior training shall complete the admission form within 10 minutes after one 30-minute session, with no more than 2 errors per form (measured in a usability test with 10 nurses). (b) The system shall be available 99.8% of clinic hours, 08:00–20:00, with planned maintenance outside them (measured from the uptime log). (c) External communication shall use TLS 1.2 or later, access permissions shall be changed only by the data administrator, and patient data shall be backed up every 24 hours to an off-site location (checked by configuration audit and a restore test). (d) 95% of lookups shall return within 2 seconds at 50 concurrent users, none over 5 seconds (measured by a load test). (e) The architecture shall support 500 concurrent users at minimum and scale to 5,000 without redesign (measured by load testing at both levels). Note the shape of every answer: subject, measurable verb, number, condition, and how it is checked.

Q4Write a complete quality attribute scenario for “the system must stay reliable during ward rounds”. Name all six parts and give the response measure.

Marker wants: all six parts labelled; a measure with a percentage and a condition; the environment distinguished from the stimulus.

Source: the ward nurse. Stimulus: opens a patient's vital-sign chart and records observations. Environment: ward rounds, 07:00–09:00, about 40 concurrent users, one database node down for maintenance. Artifact: the observation module and its database. Response: the chart loads from the replica and the observation is queued and later committed, with no data loss and no duplicate entry. Response measure: 100% of observations recorded during the failover are committed within 60 seconds of the node returning, with zero duplicates, and 95% of chart opens complete within 3 seconds. The six parts matter because a marker can see which one you skipped: a missing environment turns a conditional claim into an absolute one.

Q5Use goal decomposition to derive requirements for “reduce missed appointments”. Show every level down to a statement you could test.

Marker wants: the goal, at least one sub-goal, the NFR, and a quantitative statement; the stop rule stated.

Enterprise goal: reduce the clinic's lost appointment slots. Sub-goal: patients know about and can change their appointment in time. NFR: reminders reach patients early enough to act. Quantitative NFR: a reminder shall be delivered at least 24 hours before the slot to 99% of patients with a registered phone number, and a reschedule request shall be acknowledged within 1 minute. Then the measurable targets: deliver within a 05:00–20:00 window, retry twice on failure, and fall back to a phone call task for patients without a number. The stop rule is the deck's: keep decomposing until the statement can be measured, and keep the trace so each NFR names the goal it serves.

Q6Use concerns decomposition on “a patient is given the wrong medication”. Produce the tree, at least three interrogating questions, and the requirement each answer produces.

Marker wants: sub-concerns below the concern; questions that are answerable in requirements; one requirement per answered question.

Concern: medication error. Sub-concerns: wrong patient, wrong drug, wrong dose, wrong time. Questions and answers: (1) How does the system know which patient is in front of the nurse? — the nurse scans the bedside wristband, and the order is matched to that ID before administration is recorded. (2) What counts as the right drug when two have similar names? — the system shows generic and brand names plus the order number, and blocks selection from an unordered drug class. (3) How does the system know the dose is safe for this patient? — weight and renal function are checked against the order, and a mismatch raises a hard stop that a second nurse must override with a reason. (4) What if the dose is given late? — the administration record timestamps every dose, and a late dose beyond 60 minutes raises an alert to the ward. Each question is answered in the requirements, not deferred to the design — that is the point of the approach.

Q7Two NFRs on a shared ward tablet conflict: the lock timer must be short for security and long for usability. Decide, and justify the decision with the deck's two trade-off criteria.

Marker wants: both sides stated as quantities; a decision, not “it depends”; both criteria used; the cost named.

The conflict in numbers: a 30-second lock limits the window in which an unattended tablet exposes patient data; a 30-second lock interrupts a nurse roughly every third entry during rounds, adding re-authentication time to a task that already runs behind. Decision: lock at 2 minutes, unlock with a badge tap rather than a password, and log every chart opened with the badge ID, so the audit trail identifies the person even after the screen locks. Criterion 1 — importance: patient-data exposure on a shared device is a legal and clinical risk, so security cannot be traded away; the time-out length is negotiable, the access control is not. Criterion 2 — consequence: the 2-minute timer costs a measurable amount of security, which the badge log and per-open audit recover, while moving it back to 30 seconds costs every ward round roughly two minutes per nurse per shift. What we gave up: a strict automatic lock, in exchange for named-user traceability.

Q8A team submits: 1 use case diagram, 2 use case descriptions, 1 activity diagram with no object flow, 1 class diagram built from one use case description, 2 sequence diagrams, 1 state machine, and a UI design with no validation messages. Audit it against slide 65 and list every gap.

Marker wants: the missing item, the wrong count and the missing qualifier separated; each gap traced to the slide.

Missing: the second activity diagram, and both must include object flow — so the one submitted is short by a diagram and by a qualifier. The class diagram is short by a source: it must be built from two use case descriptions, and should apply analysis patterns. Missing entirely: the deployment diagram, the network model, and the hardware and software specification. Present but incomplete: the UI design must cover both use case descriptions and include input validation and user-interaction messages. Correct: 1 use case diagram, 2 descriptions at detail and essential level, 2 sequence diagrams, 1 state machine with its description. Report it as a checklist with three columns (present, wrong count, missing qualifier) rather than prose, because that is how the marker reads the deliverable.

Lesson 9

6 questions. Which document, which section, and how much detail.

Q1Name the three requirement specifications and what each states. Then place these four statements in the right one: (a) nurses need a patient's appointment history at the bedside; (b) the hospital information system shall expose that history through the clinical portal; (c) the portal shall show the last 12 months within 2 seconds; (d) the portal shall be verified by a load test at 50 concurrent users.

Marker wants: three definitions; four correct placements; the reason stated as “who the sentence is about”.

StRS states what the stakeholders need in their words. SyRS states what the whole system must do, hardware and people included, and fixes the interface between the system and its software portion. SRS states what the software must do, under what conditions and constraints, and how each requirement will be verified. Placement: (a) StRS — the need, not the system; (b) SyRS — an allocation to the system's software portion; (c) SRS — a measurable software requirement; (d) SRS — the verification approach, which the SyRS does not carry. The test: ask who the sentence is about — the stakeholder, the system, or the software.

Q2List the six ways IEEE 830 allows functional requirements to be organised, and apply two of them to a clinic appointment system, saying which reader each suits.

Marker wants: six named schemes with examples; two applied; a reason tied to the document's reader.

By feature (telephone: local call, call forwarding, conference call), system mode (training, normal, emergency), user class (elevator: passengers, maintenance workers, firefighters), object (patient monitoring: patients, sensors, nurses, rooms, physicians, medicines), stimulus (automatic landing: loss of power, wind shear, sudden roll, excessive vertical velocity) and response (personnel system: paychecks, employee list). For the clinic: by feature — booking, rescheduling, cancellation, reminders — suits the product owner and the test team, because each feature is a unit of delivery; by user class — patient, receptionist, doctor, administrator — suits the training team and the UI designer, because each class sees a different screen. Either is correct if you name the reader; the order is a decision, not a rule.

Q3An SRS opens with a title, a table of contents, and a single reference list. Name what the general-content section still requires, and say why each missing item matters.

Marker wants: the five items; the specific gap in each; the compliance/guidance split explained, not just named.

The section holds five things: identification, front matter, definitions, references, acronyms. Missing here: (1) a revision notice — title plus revision uniquely identify the document, and without the version, date, approval signature and list of changed subclauses nobody can tell which copy was approved; (2) the list of figures and list of tables, part of the front matter; (3) definitions for any word with a meaning beyond the dictionary — in a clinical SRS that includes “patient”, “encounter” and “result”; (4) the compliance / guidance split in the references — compliance covers cited documents whose requirements are included by the citation, guidance covers documents that inform but impose nothing; merging them hides what the software must satisfy; (5) an acronym list — HL7, MLLP, ORU, PDPA.

Q4Name the eight constraints under product perspective, and classify each item: hospital Wi-Fi with WPA2-Enterprise; a USB barcode scanner on the bedside tablet; the lab system's HL7 v2.5.1 interface; a 2 GB memory minimum; ward-specific bed labels and printer names; unattended overnight synchronisation.

Marker wants: the eight named in order; six correct mappings; the difference between user and system interface stated.

The eight: system interfaces, user interfaces, hardware interfaces, software interfaces, communications interfaces, memory, operations, site adaptation. Mapping: Wi-Fi with WPA2-Enterprise — communications interfaces. USB barcode scanner — hardware interfaces. The lab system's HL7 version — software interfaces, with the other product's name, mnemonic, specification number, version and source plus message content and format. 2 GB minimum — memory. Ward-specific labels and printer names — site adaptation. Overnight synchronisation — operations, which also covers interactive versus unattended periods and backup and recovery. The distinction that earns the last mark: user interfaces are human-computer and belong here; system interfaces are machine-machine and belong to systems integration.

Q5Rewrite this performance requirement so it can be tested: “The appointment system shall respond quickly under heavy use so that receptionists are not delayed.” Separate the static from the dynamic requirement.

Marker wants: two requirements; numbers with conditions; a load named; the 95th percentile or equivalent.

Static (capacity): the system shall support 120 receptionist terminals and 300 simultaneous users, holding 12 months of appointment history online. Dynamic: 95% of appointment lookups shall complete in under 1 second at 50 concurrent users during clinic hours, and 99% in under 3 seconds at peak load, with no lookup exceeding 5 seconds. Verification: a 30-minute load test at both levels, measuring the 95th and 99th percentile response times. Note the deck's own contrast: “95% of the transactions shall be processed in less than 1 second” is a requirement; “an operator shall not have to wait” is not, because it contains no number and no condition.

Q6An SRS team submits: general content complete; product perspective complete; product functions and user characteristics written; no limitations, assumptions, or apportioning; specific requirements done; maintainability stated as “the code shall be modular and well documented”; no verification section. List every gap against the outline and say what each one costs.

Marker wants: gaps grouped by container; the maintainability warning quoted in substance; verification described as parallel, not appended.

Product overview — missing three sections: limitations (regulatory policy, hardware timing, interfaces to other applications, audit, quality, criticality, safety and security), assumptions and dependencies (factors that are not design constraints but whose change would change the requirements, such as the Wi-Fi assumption), and apportioning (which requirements belong to which software element, with a cross-reference table; state explicitly where the allocation is undefined). Without them, a change in an assumption arrives as a surprise rather than a change to the SRS. Software system attributes — wrong content: “the code shall be modular and well documented” is exactly what the deck warns against — requirements do not belong there just because they are thought to be good design practice. Replace it with a measurable maintainability requirement or move it to design constraints. Missing verification: required, and written in parallel with sections 3.1–3.10, not appended; each requirement needs its test approach beside it. Correct: general content, product perspective, product functions, user characteristics, and the specific requirements.

Lesson 10

8 questions. Prototype choice, screen critique, and requirements a tester can run.

Q1Explain the difference between using a prototype for elicitation and for validation, and give one concrete outcome of each in a hospital project.

Marker wants: the two purposes separated; an outcome that could only come from each; the success test named.

Elicitation uses the prototype to let users experiment with how the system supports their work, find strengths and weaknesses, and propose requirements that are hard to describe in words. Its success test is that new requirements appear. Validation uses the prototype to test the requirements you already have; testing uncovers mistakes and missing details, and users realise their earlier expectations were inaccurate or incomplete. Its success test is that wrong or missing requirements are removed before the build. Outcomes: elicitation — the ward asks for a “today's list” view that appears in no interview; validation — the same ward discovers the admission flow it asked for takes six clicks and asks for it to be collapsed. A single session can produce both, but the report must say which question it was answering.

Q2Run a validation session for a ward tablet that records vital signs. Give the four steps, and for each say what you would actually do and what you would write down.

Marker wants: the four steps in order; the user working alone; the observer's record; the output of the session.

(1) Choose testers: three nurses who have used at least one clinical system and are open to a new one — not the ward's most resistant nurse, and not the IT champion. (2) Develop scenarios covering a broad range of requirements: record routine observations; record an out-of-range reading that triggers an alert; record with no network; hand over a patient mid-round. (3) Execute: each nurse works alone at the bedside while you observe and say nothing; you note every hesitation, wrong tap and re-read with a timestamp. (4) Document: a numbered list of problems, each with the scenario, what the nurse did, what the design expected, and the change it implies. The output is the evaluation report from the prototype model, and it feeds the requirements, not the code.

Q3Choose evolutionary or throwaway for each, and justify with the deck's criteria: (a) an AI triage assistant whose behaviour is only understood once it runs; (b) a replacement for a laboratory interface that must follow a fixed HL7 profile; (c) a patient booking web site for a new private clinic.

Marker wants: the choice; whether the requirements are knowable in advance; what is kept at the end.

(a) Evolutionary — open-ended, because the behaviour cannot be specified in advance; the deck names AI as the case, and what is kept is the working system, often with no detailed specification. (b) Throwaway — the requirements are fixed by the HL7 profile, so the prototype exists to confirm edge cases and error handling; what is kept is the specification, and the prototype is discarded, with quality relaxed and performance ignored because it will not ship. (c) Evolutionary — the deck says this is now the normal technique for web sites and e-commerce, and the requirement set will change as the clinic learns; what is kept is the site. The test behind all three: are the requirements knowable before you build, and do you intend to keep the artefact or the document?

Q4Critique this screen using the six principles: a ward dashboard with no title and no “last updated” time; vital signs in one large table, appointments in another, and the alert list floating in the middle; a red alert label on a blue background; “Appointment” in the menu and “Booking” on the form; reaching a patient's history takes five taps; the same concept uses two different icons on different screens.

Marker wants: each fault tied to a named principle; no unnamed taste; a fix for each.

Content awareness: no title and no “last updated” means the nurse cannot tell what the screen is or how old the numbers are — add a title and a preparation time. Layout: the alert list floating between two tables breaks the grouping rule — give it its own area, and order the areas by the task. Aesthetics: red on blue is the deck's own example of a colour pair that fails; use a contrast-checked pair. Consistency: “Appointment” and “Booking” for the same object, and two icons for one concept — pick one term and one icon and apply them everywhere. Minimal user effort: five taps to the history exceeds the three-click rule; surface the history from the patient row. User experience: decide whether this is a novice or an expert screen — if novices use it, the density and the unlabelled icons both need work. Name the principle before the criticism; that is what is marked.

Q5Draw or describe a window navigation diagram for booking an appointment: main menu, appointment list, booking form, confirmation. Say which transitions need a return and which do not, and why.

Marker wants: boxes typed by stereotype; single versus double arrows justified; no invented screen.

Boxes: «window» Main menu → «window» Appointments → «form» Booking → «window» Confirmation. Transitions: Main menu ⇄ Appointments, double, because the user must be able to come back to the menu; Appointments ⇄ Booking, double, because cancelling the form returns to the list; Booking → Confirmation, single, because the confirmation is a terminal screen for that task; Confirmation ⇄ Appointments, double, because the user returns to the list after reading it. The rule is a claim about behaviour, not decoration: a double arrow says the user is required to return to the calling state, so draw it only where that is true. Add the use-case scenario beside the diagram; the WND is documented with the real use cases.

Q6Pick the evaluation approach for each situation and say why the others do not fit: (a) a paper storyboard reviewed by the design team against Nielsen's heuristics; (b) three nurses trying a clickable prototype alone while you watch; (c) a timed task in a lab with screen and keystroke recording.

Marker wants: three correct methods; the fidelity restriction quoted; the evidence each produces.

(a) Heuristic evaluation — a formal checklist applied to the design by the team; the storyboard is not clickable, so interactive and formal testing are impossible. (b) Interactive evaluation — one user at a time works through the real use cases while a team member records hesitation, mistakes and misinterpretation; this is the method the deck restricts: it cannot be used with storyboards or window layout diagrams, and the prototype must be clickable. (c) Formal usability testing — in a lab, alone, with video and keystroke and mouse recording, using a language prototype. A walkthrough — the team presenting the prototype and explaining it — fits any fidelity but produces opinion, not observed behaviour, so it is the weakest evidence of the three. Choose by the question: checklist → heuristic; watch a user work → interactive; measure → formal test.

Q7Apply the six validation checks to a patient registration form, with one concrete failure for each.

Marker wants: six named checks in the deck's order; a specific field and a specific bad value for each.

Completeness: surname left empty — the form must not submit. Format: a Thai national ID typed as 13 characters including a letter, or a date as 31/02/2026. Range: age 250, or a temperature of 9 °C in a field that accepts 30–45. Check digit: a 13-digit national ID whose final digit does not match the checksum. Consistency: a discharge date earlier than the admission date, or a phone number whose country code contradicts the selected address. Database check: the national ID already exists under another patient record, which would violate a uniqueness constraint. Two additions the deck implies: validation runs before entry, and the message is written in plain language that names the problem and the fix — “National ID already registered to a patient in this ward”, not “Error 409”.

Q8Take this NFR — “the ward app must be usable one-handed by a nurse holding a tablet” — and turn it into a UI requirement, an effect on the screen design, and a Given / When / Then acceptance criterion. Then name the NFR family it belongs to.

Marker wants: four columns in order; a screen effect that is visible; a criterion with situation, action and observable outcome.

Family: operational, with an accessibility element — the constraint is the device and how it is held. UI requirement: the primary action of every ward screen shall sit within the lower third of the screen and be reachable by the thumb of the hand holding the device; all touch targets at least 44 pixels. Effect on screen design: the “Record” button spans the bottom edge, secondary actions move into a top bar, and no primary action depends on a drag or a long press. Acceptance criterion: Given a nurse holding the tablet in one hand at the bedside, when recording a set of vital signs, then every required action is completable with that hand without putting the tablet down. The same four-column shape works for the deck's own rows: operational, performance, security and cultural, each ending in a sentence a tester can run.

Lesson 11

6 questions. Validate the document, then keep it true.

Q1Distinguish requirements validation from requirements verification, and say what each asks at the three levels the deck names.

Marker wants: the two definitions in the deck's own terms; the three levels; one sentence showing a document can pass one and fail the other.

Validation defines the right software — the software that conforms to what users need and expect. Verification checks that the requirements conform to the organisation's standard and carry the characteristics of a good requirement: consistency, clarity, completeness. Both apply at three levels: the specification document (is the whole thing complete and consistent?), the set of requirements (does the set cover the need with no gap or duplicate, and is each item traceable?), and an individual requirement (is it well formed, and is it what the user meant?). The two columns are independent: “The system shall answer a lookup within 2 seconds” is well formed and measurable — verification passes — but if the ward needs it at the bedside in under a second, validation fails.

Q2Name the four fundamental validation practices, and choose one for each situation: a 200-page SRS nobody has read; a workflow the nurses cannot describe in words; a class diagram whose objects never appear on any sequence diagram; a requirement about alarm latency.

Marker wants: the four names; the right practice per situation; the reason tied to what each practice can see.

The four: requirements review, prototyping, model validation, acceptance testing. Situations: the unread SRS — review, with a checklist and at least one customer representative on the panel; the workflow nobody can describe — prototyping, because dynamic behaviour is easier to judge from an animated prototype than from prose; the class objects that never appear in a sequence diagram — model validation, a static analysis of communication paths across the structural and behavioural models; the alarm-latency requirement — acceptance testing, after the NFR is decomposed to a measurable threshold (“alarm raised within 1 second of the reading crossing the limit”). A review finds what is written wrongly, a prototype finds what was never written, model validation finds two models that disagree, and an acceptance test decides whether the finished product meets the sentence.

Q3What goes into the summary report of an SRS review, and why is the results table two-dimensional?

Marker wants: the eight contents; the reason for the matrix shape; what a cell holds.

The report carries: the objective of the review; its scope, meaning the document under revision; the participants, reviewed by whom; date and time; terms and definitions, including a list of defect types; the checklist; the results; and the open issues with the action on each and who is responsible, with an explanation for every reviewed item. The results table is two-dimensional because a review is not one verdict: rows are checklist items, columns are the requirements reviewed, and each cell holds Pass, Fail or Notes with the specified reason and the way to solve it. That shape lets a reader see both which requirement is weak and which kind of defect keeps appearing — the defect-type list is what makes the results comparable between reviews.

Q4Classify each defect, then rewrite two of them: (a) “The system shall store data securely.” (b) “The system shall support up to 500 users and unlimited concurrent users.” (c) “The app shall verify the fingerprint against a national database in 0.01 ms.” (d) “The system shall delete old records.”

Marker wants: four correct labels; rewrites that add a number, a condition or a named control — not a synonym.

(a) Ambiguous and incomplete — “securely” names no control and no scope. (b) Contradictory — 500 and unlimited cannot both hold. (c) Infeasible — a network round trip and a matching algorithm cannot finish in 0.01 ms. (d) Incomplete — “old” is undefined and the linked data is unaddressed. Rewrites: (a) “The system shall encrypt data in transit with TLS 1.2 or later and at rest with AES-256, and shall allow access only to users holding the treating-clinician role.” (c) “The app shall authenticate the user with on-device biometric hardware and grant access within 500 ms of a successful scan.” Note the pattern the deck uses in all four of its examples: the repair adds a number, a condition, or a named standard — never a better adjective.

Q5A use case description records four events; its activity diagram shows five actions, one of which is “check insurance”; the diagram also contains an object, InsurancePolicy, that no event mentions. Which of the eight verification rules fail, and what are the two possible repairs?

Marker wants: the rules by name; the two repairs stated as “fix the description” or “fix the diagram”; the reason it is a requirements defect.

Rule 1 fails: every action or activity on the activity diagram needs one recorded event in the flows of the use-case description, and “check insurance” has none. Rule 2 fails: every object in the activity diagram must be mentioned in an event, and InsurancePolicy is not. If the actions are also out of order, rule 3 fails as well, and rule 4 would fail if a second description existed for the same use case. Repairs: either the description is incomplete — add the event that checks insurance and names the policy object — or the diagram is wrong — remove an action the use case never performs. The choice is a requirements decision, not a drawing decision: the two models are one description seen twice, so the mismatch means the requirements are not yet settled. Then re-check rules 5 to 8: actors on the diagram, stakeholders per local policy, relationships drawn, and diagram-specific syntax.

Q6A clinic asks, three weeks before release, to move the cancellation window from 48 to 24 hours. Walk the change through requirements management: which baseline it touches, what tracing tells you, and which attributes you update.

Marker wants: the baseline named; backward and forward tracing used; the attribute groups touched; the creep risk stated.

Baseline: it changes a reviewed system requirement, so it touches the functional baseline, and once built it also touches the product baseline — two different approval authorities, both named in the configuration management plan. It goes in as a change request with an impact assessment, review and approval, not as an edit. Tracing: backward, the requirement traces to its source — the board policy or the clinic manager's goal; forward, it traces to the cancellation screen, the two test cases (cancel before and after the window) and the manual paragraph, all of which must change in the same release. Attributes: identifier stays, version increments, change history records who changed what and why, the verification method and acceptance-test links are updated, priority and owner are confirmed, and the traceability links are re-pointed at the new test cases. Creep: one approved request is management; the same request arriving unlogged, three weeks before release, with nobody assessing its cost, is requirements creep — the deck's list of consequences starts at cost overrun and ends at cancellation.

Lesson 12

6 questions. Place the logic, choose the architecture, draw what runs where.

Q1What does the physical architecture layer decide, and what does the deck say about the role of non-functional requirements in it?

Marker wants: the two decisions; the NFR sentence in the deck's terms (design goal, acceptance, technology choice); the three deliverables it names.

มันตัดสินสองอย่าง: ระบบถูกกระจายไปบนเครื่องคอมพิวเตอร์อย่างไร และจะใช้อุปกรณ์และซอฟต์แวร์อะไร ทั้งสองอย่างถูกจำกัดด้วยระบบและเครือข่ายที่มีอยู่แล้ว ส่วนบทบาทของ NFR ตามสไลด์ 5 คือ: การออกแบบ การพัฒนา และการติดตั้งต้องสอดคล้องกับ NFR, NFR ถูกใช้เป็นเป้าหมายการออกแบบและเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของการตรวจรับระบบ และเทคโนโลยีที่เลือกขึ้นกับ NFR — ซึ่งแยกออกเป็นสามผลลัพธ์คือ system/software architecture, hardware และ software specification และ user interface design (บทถัดไป) พูดให้สั้น: physical architecture คือที่ที่ NFR กลายเป็นการตัดสินใจที่จับต้องได้

Q2Name the four software logics, then say where each sits in: a mainframe terminal, a clinic with the program installed on every reception PC and the database on a shared drive, a browser-only web client, and a tablet that records sessions offline and syncs later.

Marker wants: the four logics; four correct placements; thin vs thick decided by where the logic sits, not by the device.

logic สี่ตัวคือ data storage, data access logic, application logic และ presentation logic การวาง: (1) mainframe terminal — server-based เพราะทั้งสี่ logic อยู่ที่ server ส่วน terminal ส่งแค่ keystroke; (2) คลินิกที่ติดตั้งโปรแกรมบนเครื่อง reception ทุกเครื่องและฐานข้อมูลอยู่บน shared drive — client-based เพราะ client ทำ access, application และ presentation ส่วน server เป็น file server เก็บ data storage อย่างเดียว; (3) browser-only web client — thin client-server เพราะ client ทำ presentation อย่างเดียว; (4) แท็บเล็ตที่บันทึก session แบบ offline แล้วค่อย sync — thick client-server เพราะ application logic บางส่วนลงมาอยู่ที่ client ด้วย และการ sync กลายเป็น requirement ทางสถาปัตยกรรม เกณฑ์ตัดสินคือ “logic อยู่ที่ไหน” ไม่ใช่ว่าเครื่องเป็นอะไร

Q3A private clinic with no capital budget, one developer and a requirement to grow to five branches within two years must choose an architecture. Use the six criteria, take a position, and name what you give up.

Marker wants: the six criteria named; a decision; the losing column stated; the growth requirement used as evidence.

เกณฑ์หกข้อ: cost of acquisition, cost of development, ease of development, interface capabilities, control and security, scalability คำตอบที่สมเหตุสมผลคือ client-server เพราะคอลัมน์นี้ได้ค่าอุปกรณ์ต่ำ (low infrastructure cost) และ scalability สูง ซึ่งตรงกับเงื่อนไข “ขยายเป็นห้าสาขาในสองปี” และได้ interface capabilities สูงซึ่งจำเป็นกับหน้าจอผู้ป่วย สิ่งที่ต้องแลกคือ cost of development สูง — ต้องเขียนทั้งฝั่ง client และ server — และ control/security อยู่ระดับกลาง ซึ่งต้องชดเชยด้วย NFR ด้าน security แยก (TLS, RBAC, audit log) ถ้าโรงพยาบาลมีทีมเดียวและงบจำกัดจริง ๆ การเลือก server-based จะคุม security ได้ดีกว่าและค่าโครงสร้างพื้นฐานสูง แต่ cost of development สูงตามที่ครูแก้ในคลาส และ scalability ต่ำ จึงไม่ตรงกับเงื่อนไขการขยาย

Q4For a clinic web application with a browser, a web server, an application server and a database, how many tiers is it, what sits in each, and what does each extra tier buy?

Marker wants: the tier count from the logic split; what each machine holds; the benefit and the cost of the extra tier.

ระบบนี้เป็น n-tier (สี่ชั้น) ตามคำจำกัดความของสไลด์: ชั้นที่ 1 browser — presentation logic; ชั้นที่ 2 web server — ให้บริการหน้าเว็บและตัด TLS; ชั้นที่ 3 application server — application logic; ชั้นที่ 4 database server — data storage และ data access logic การแยก web server ออกมาเพิ่มจาก 3-tier ซื้ออะไร: (ก) แยกจุดที่รับ traffic จากอินเทอร์เน็ตออกจากที่ประมวลผลธุรกิจ จึงวาง web server ใน DMZ และปิด port อื่นได้ (ข) ทำ load balancing ได้ง่ายกว่า และ (ค) อัปเดต application โดยไม่ต้องแตะ web tier สิ่งที่เสียคือ ความซับซ้อนและจำนวนเครื่องที่ต้องดูแลเพิ่มขึ้น และ network latency ระหว่างชั้น — สอดคล้องกับที่สไลด์บอกว่า n-tier “places higher demands on the network”

Q5A clinic group has a head office and two branches. Describe the two network-model diagrams you would draw and what each one is used for.

Marker wants: the two passes in order; what belongs at each level; the link from the low-level diagram to the hardware list.

รอบแรก top-level: วาดสาม node คือสำนักงานใหญ่กับสองสาขา และเส้นเชื่อมระหว่างที่ พร้อมกำกับชนิดและต้นทุนของเส้น (leased line, VPN ผ่านอินเทอร์เน็ต) รอบนี้ตอบว่า “มีกี่ที่ อยู่ห่างกันแค่ไหน และค่าการสื่อสารจะแพงแค่ไหน” จึงใช้ตัดสินงบโครงข่าย รอบที่สอง low-level: วาดแยกทีละที่ ลงรายละเอียดภายใน เช่น ที่สาขาหนึ่งมี switch, application server, database server และเครื่องลูกข่ายตามจำนวนห้องตรวจ รอบนี้ตอบว่า “ในแต่ละที่มีอุปกรณ์อะไร” และเป็นจุดตั้งต้นของ hardware specification ตามสไลด์ 33 — ชนิดและจำนวน server, peripheral, storage และ backup ต่อที่ ข้อผิดพลาดที่พบบ่อยคือเอาอุปกรณ์ทั้งหมดไปใส่ในรอบแรก ทำให้ภาพระดับภูมิศาสตร์กลายเป็นภาพระดับเครื่อง

Q6Take the two NFRs from the assignment — availability and security — and state, for each, the requirement as a number and the architectural mechanism it forces. Then name where each mechanism appears on a deployment diagram.

Marker wants: number first, mechanism second; a concrete node or path for each; the point that the NFR is the reason for the structure.

Availability: requirement — พร้อมใช้งาน 99.5% ของเวลาทำการ และกู้คืนภายใน 5 นาที; mechanism — กำจัด single point of failure ด้วย load balancer และ application server สองตัวหลังมัน, ฐานข้อมูลที่มี replica และ backup; บน deployment diagram จะเห็นเป็น node «device» load balancer และ «execution environment» application servers (2) พร้อม artifact เดียวกันติดตั้งทั้งสองตัว Security: requirement — PII เข้ารหัสทั้ง at rest และ in transit และไม่เก็บเลขบัตร; mechanism — TLS ทุกเส้น, gateway ของบริษัทบัตรอยู่นอกขอบเขต, masking ที่ presentation layer, log และ RBAC; บนแผนภาพจะเห็นเป็น communication path ที่กำกับ HTTPS ทุกเส้น และ node «device» external ที่อยู่นอก boundary ประโยคปิดที่ได้คะแนน: ถ้าลบ NFR สองข้อออก แผนภาพจะเหลือ node เดียวต่อชั้นและเส้นที่ไม่ต้องระบุ protocol — แปลว่าโครงสร้างที่เห็นคือคำตอบของ NFR ไม่ใช่ของแฟชั่นสถาปัตยกรรม

Self-marking multiple choice

Mock test

Fifteen questions from the scope you pick, marked on submit, each with the reason. The midterm scope is Lessons 1–6; the final scope is everything after the midterm, Lessons 6–12, and includes the sixteen Part 1 items of the Mock final.

Practice paper · post-midterm scope

Mock final

One full paper in the shape the lecturer described: Part 1 multiple choice (16 marks), Part 2 nine written questions on one case (44 marks), Part 3 modelling (20 marks). Sit it in three hours with one computer and no internet, then reveal.

Where this paper comes from. The structure, the four diagram types, and the two case domains — Smart Farm for the long case and Robotaxi for goal decomposition — follow the study document SRE-สิ่งที่อาจารย์บอกว่าออกสอบ-แยกตามบท, compiled from a clip that is not in this project. Your own 24 Nov recording names an Online Ticket Reservation case instead, so practise the method, not the domain. Every question was checked against a deck slide or a class recording; topics she said are not examined (sync/async messages, entity-control-boundary, network model, cloud, hardware tables) are left out.

Suggested timing (180 min): Part 1 · 20 min · Part 2 · 100 min · Part 3 · 50 min · re-read · 10 min.

ข้อสอบจำลองชุดเต็มตามโครงที่อาจารย์บอก: Part 1 ปรนัย 16 คะแนน · Part 2 ข้อเขียนเก้าข้อจากกรณีเดียว 44 คะแนน · Part 3 สร้างแบบจำลอง 20 คะแนน (class, sequence, state machine, deployment) โดเมนตามเอกสารเตรียมสอบคือ Smart Farm และ Robotaxi แต่ไฟล์เสียงวันที่ 24 พ.ย. พูดถึง Online Ticket Reservation จึงควรฝึกวิธีคิดมากกว่าจำโดเมน

Part 1 — accuracy, 16 marks

Sixteen items, one mark each; some need a step of analysis. The same items are in the Mock test tab under the final scope, where they mark themselves.

1Which operation belongs in an analysis-level class diagram for the Smart Farm?

  1. getCrop()
  2. setStatus()
  3. recordHarvest()
  4. createPlot()

1 mark · Lesson 6

(c) recordHarvest(). Get/set and create/delete are assumed for every class and omitted; recordHarvest() is a problem-domain operation. get/set และ create/delete ละไว้เพราะทุกคลาสทำได้อยู่แล้ว recordHarvest() เป็น operation ของ problem domain

2A plot's /totalYield is shown with a leading slash because it is:

  1. private
  2. static
  3. optional
  4. derived from other attributes

1 mark · Lesson 6

(d) derived from other attributes. A slash marks a derived attribute — here the sum of the plot's lots. Private is the minus sign. slash นำหน้า = derived attribute (คำนวณจากผลรวมของ lot) ส่วน private คือเครื่องหมายลบ

3Textual analysis of “each greenhouse has many plots” points to:

  1. aggregation or composition
  2. generalisation
  3. a constraint
  4. an operation

1 mark · Lesson 6

(a) aggregation or composition. A having verb maps to aggregation or composition; decide logical (aggregation) or physical (composition) next. having verb → aggregation หรือ composition แล้วค่อยดูว่าเป็นเชิง logical หรือ physical

4A message that :Plot receives on a sequence diagram must exist as:

  1. an attribute of Plot
  2. an operation of Plot in the class diagram
  3. a state of Plot
  4. a separate actor

1 mark · Lesson 7

(b) an operation of Plot in the class diagram. A received message is an operation of the receiving class; if the class diagram lacks it, go back and add it. message ที่ object รับต้องเป็น operation ของคลาสนั้น ถ้าไม่มีต้องกลับไปเพิ่มใน class diagram

5“Record harvest” includes “Generate QR code”. On the sequence diagram the included behaviour is drawn as:

  1. ref, placed where it is called, outside any alt
  2. ref inside an opt
  3. an asynchronous message
  4. a second sequence diagram with no link

1 mark · Lesson 7

(a) ref, placed where it is called, outside any alt. Include is mandatory, so the ref is always called at its point in the flow; extend is the conditional one. include บังคับเรียกเสมอ จึงเป็น ref ที่ตำแหน่งที่เรียก ส่วน extend มีเงื่อนไขจึงอยู่ใน alt/opt

6Which is NOT one of the deck's three kinds of event that trigger a transition?

  1. a designated condition becoming true
  2. receipt of a signal from another object
  3. passage of a designated time
  4. an attribute of the object being read

1 mark · Lesson 7

(d) an attribute of the object being read. The three are condition, signal and time. Reading a value changes nothing, so it cannot move the state. event มีสามแบบ: เงื่อนไขเป็นจริง · signal · เวลาผ่านไป การอ่านค่าไม่เปลี่ยน state

7What does a behavioural state machine help an analyst validate?

  1. the network topology
  2. the colour scheme
  3. the completeness of the functional requirements
  4. the database index plan

1 mark · Lesson 7

(c) the completeness of the functional requirements. Every transition needs an actor action from a use case; a state no use case can reach means a missing function. state machine ช่วยตรวจว่า functional requirement ครบ — ถ้ามี state ที่ไม่มี use case ไหนพาไปถึง แปลว่าขาด function

8“The buyer's certification scheme requires chemical records to be kept for 2 years” is best classified as:

  1. an external requirement stated as a fact
  2. a process requirement
  3. a functional requirement
  4. a usability requirement

1 mark · Lesson 8

(a) an external requirement stated as a fact. External requirements arrive as facts and rules of the outside world; the analyst turns them into capabilities. external requirement มาในรูปข้อเท็จจริงหรือกฎภายนอก นักวิเคราะห์ต้องแปลงเป็นความสามารถของระบบ

9Which ordering is the deck's goal decomposition?

  1. NFR → goal → sub-goal → metric
  2. use case → goal → NFR
  3. metric → NFR → goal
  4. goal → sub-goal → NFR → quantitative NFR

1 mark · Lesson 8

(d) goal → sub-goal → NFR → quantitative NFR. Goal decomposition runs from the enterprise goal down until the statement can be measured, which keeps it traceable. goal → sub-goal → NFR → quantitative NFR และตามรอยกลับไปหา goal ขององค์กรได้

10“Protect customer data from unauthorised access” becomes a functional requirement when it is rewritten as:

  1. “security shall be high”
  2. “log in with a password and a 6-digit SMS code”
  3. “data shall be safe”
  4. “follow good practice”

1 mark · Lesson 8

(b) “log in with a password and a 6-digit SMS code”. The FR/NFR boundary moves with the level of detail: concrete steps the developers must build make it functional. เส้นแบ่ง FR/NFR ขยับตาม level of detail — พอเป็นขั้นตอนที่ต้องสร้างจริงก็กลายเป็น FR

11“The dashboard shall be easy to use” fails because it is not:

  1. functional
  2. short
  3. objective and testable
  4. written in Thai

1 mark · Lesson 8

(c) objective and testable. An NFR must be objective and testable; rewrite it with a measure such as time to learn or errors per hour. NFR ต้อง objective และ testable — เขียนใหม่ด้วยตัววัด เช่น เวลาเรียนรู้หรือจำนวน error

12A paper storyboard of the harvest screens can be evaluated by:

  1. interactive evaluation
  2. formal usability testing in a lab
  3. heuristic evaluation
  4. keystroke logging

1 mark · Lesson 10

(c) heuristic evaluation. Interactive evaluation and formal testing need something the user can operate; a storyboard supports heuristic review or a walkthrough. storyboard ใช้ interactive หรือ formal testing ไม่ได้ ต้องเป็น heuristic หรือ walkthrough

13Rejecting a harvest date earlier than the plot's planting date is which validation check?

  1. format
  2. range
  3. check digit
  4. consistency

1 mark · Lesson 10

(d) consistency. It compares two related data items, which is a consistency check; a range check tests one value against fixed bounds. เทียบข้อมูลสองตัวที่สัมพันธ์กัน = consistency check ส่วน range คือค่าเดียวเทียบกับขอบเขตคงที่

14“Printing label… tap Cancel to stop” is which message type?

  1. delay
  2. acknowledgment
  3. confirmation
  4. help

1 mark · Lesson 10

(a) delay. A delay message says the process is running; the deck adds that it should let the user cancel. delay message บอกว่ากำลังทำงานอยู่ และควรให้ผู้ใช้ยกเลิกได้

15In a requirements review, a requirement with no identifier and no source fails which checklist group?

  1. organisation and structure
  2. traceability
  3. special issues
  4. aesthetics

1 mark · Lesson 11

(b) traceability. Traceability asks for a unique ID and a traceable source; without them no change can be tracked. traceability ต้องมี ID เฉพาะและตามรอยกลับไปหาแหล่งที่มาได้

16In a web-based 3-tier deployment diagram, the DBMS and the farm schema are:

  1. nodes of their own
  2. artifacts on the database server node
  3. communication paths
  4. stereotypes of the client

1 mark · Lesson 12

(b) artifacts on the database server node. Software is an artifact and cannot stand alone; it sits on the node that runs it. ซอฟต์แวร์และ schema เป็น artifact อยู่ลำพังไม่ได้ ต้องอยู่บน node

Part 2 — written answers on one case, 44 marks

Read the case once, index it, then answer. Q2 uses its own short Robotaxi prompt.

Case — GreenLeaf Smart Farm (a fictional company; all numbers are part of the case)

GreenLeaf grows hydroponic vegetables in four greenhouses in Nakhon Pathom and wants a web-based Smart Farm system used by the owner, the farm manager, workers on tablets, and wholesale buyers on their phones.

  1. Each greenhouse is divided into plots. Each plot has sensors (water level in the growing channel, temperature, humidity, nutrient EC, pH, light) that send a reading every 5 minutes through an on-site LoRaWAN gateway.
  2. The farm manager sets a growing plan per plot: the crop, the planting date, and a target range for each sensor type.
  3. When a reading stays outside its target range for more than 10 minutes, the system raises an alert and notifies the farm manager through an external messaging service (LINE or SMS). If nobody acknowledges it within 30 minutes, the owner is notified as well.
  4. Irrigation valves open and close automatically by the plan, or a worker opens them manually from a tablet. Every command is logged with who sent it and when.
  5. Workers record tasks — fertilising, pest inspection — and harvests: the plot, the date, the quantity in kilograms and a grade (A, B or C). Only a plot whose status is READY can be harvested.
  6. Each harvest creates a lot with a QR code. A buyer who scans it sees the plot, the planting date and the chemicals used. The buyer sees no personal data.
  7. The buyers' certification scheme requires every chemical and fertiliser record of a lot to be kept for at least 2 years and shown to an auditor on request.
  8. The owner views a monthly dashboard of yield per plot and water use.
  9. The system reads a rain forecast from an external weather service and skips scheduled irrigation when rain probability is 70% or more — unless the channel's water level is already below the plan's minimum.

กรณีศึกษา GreenLeaf Smart Farm (บริษัทสมมติ): ฟาร์มผักไฮโดรโปนิกส์สี่โรงเรือนที่นครปฐม ต้องการระบบ web-based สำหรับเจ้าของ ผู้จัดการฟาร์ม คนงาน (แท็บเล็ต) และผู้ซื้อขายส่ง (มือถือ) — (1) แต่ละโรงเรือนแบ่งเป็นแปลง มีเซนเซอร์ (ระดับน้ำในรางปลูก อุณหภูมิ ความชื้น ค่า EC ของสารละลาย pH แสง) ส่งค่าทุก 5 นาทีผ่าน LoRaWAN gateway (2) ผู้จัดการตั้งแผนการปลูกต่อแปลง: พืช วันปลูก และช่วงค่าเป้าหมาย (3) ถ้าค่าอยู่นอกช่วงเกิน 10 นาที ระบบสร้าง alert แจ้งผู้จัดการผ่าน LINE/SMS ถ้าไม่มีใครรับใน 30 นาที แจ้งเจ้าของด้วย (4) วาล์วน้ำเปิดปิดอัตโนมัติตามแผน หรือคนงานสั่งเองได้ ทุกคำสั่งบันทึกว่าใครสั่งเมื่อไร (5) คนงานบันทึกงานและการเก็บเกี่ยว: แปลง วันที่ จำนวน กก. และเกรด A/B/C เก็บได้เฉพาะแปลงสถานะ READY (6) ทุกการเก็บเกี่ยวสร้าง lot พร้อม QR ผู้ซื้อสแกนเห็นแปลง วันปลูก และสารเคมีที่ใช้ แต่ไม่เห็นข้อมูลส่วนบุคคล (7) มาตรฐานรับรองของผู้ซื้อกำหนดให้เก็บบันทึกสารเคมีและปุ๋ยของทุก lot อย่างน้อย 2 ปี และแสดงต่อผู้ตรวจได้ (8) เจ้าของดู dashboard รายเดือน (9) ระบบอ่านพยากรณ์ฝนจากบริการภายนอก ถ้าโอกาสฝน ≥ 70% ให้ข้ามการรดน้ำ เว้นแต่ระดับน้ำในรางต่ำกว่าเกณฑ์ขั้นต่ำแล้ว

Q1The owner's main concern is crop loss from water stress. Using concerns decomposition, break the concern down and declare at least three functional requirements that can be measured. (5 marks)เจ้าของกังวลเรื่องพืชเสียหายจากการขาดหรือเกินน้ำ จงใช้ concerns decomposition แตกประเด็น แล้วระบุ functional requirement ที่วัดได้อย่างน้อยสามข้อ

Use Lesson 8 · clause 7 · Lesson 11 memo (42:47, the Sky Train example)

Marker wants: the concern broken into sub-concerns and causes; the questions asked at each branch; at least three requirements, each with a condition, a number and a response.

แตกประเด็น (concern → sub-concern → สาเหตุ): crop loss from water stress → (ก) ขาดน้ำ — ระดับน้ำในรางต่ำ (ข) น้ำเกิน — น้ำล้นรางหรือปั๊มไม่หยุด → สาเหตุ: วาล์วค้างปิดหรือค้างเปิด, เซนเซอร์ระดับน้ำเสียหรือเงียบ, แผนรดน้ำไม่ตรงกับสภาพอากาศ, gateway หรือเครือข่ายล่ม

คำถามที่ต้องตอบทีละกิ่ง: “ขาดน้ำ” วัดจากระดับน้ำในราง ต่ำกว่าเท่าไร นานเท่าไร? ระบบรู้ได้อย่างไรว่าวาล์วไม่ทำงานจริง? ถ้าเซนเซอร์เงียบ ระบบควรถือว่าเป็นความเสี่ยงหรือไม่?

Functional requirement ที่วัดได้: (1) เมื่อระดับน้ำในรางของแปลงใดต่ำกว่าค่าต่ำสุดของแผนติดต่อกัน 10 นาที ระบบต้องเปิดวาล์วของแปลงนั้นภายใน 1 นาที และแจ้งผู้จัดการภายใน 2 นาที (2) หลังสั่งเปิดวาล์ว ถ้า flow sensor ไม่รายงานการไหลภายใน 2 นาที ระบบต้องตั้งสถานะวาล์วเป็น FAULTY และส่ง alert (3) ถ้าเซนเซอร์ตัวใดไม่ส่งค่า 3 รอบติดกัน (15 นาที) ระบบต้องสร้าง alert “sensor silent” (4) เมื่อโอกาสฝน ≥ 70% ระบบข้ามการรดน้ำตามตาราง ยกเว้นระดับน้ำต่ำกว่าเกณฑ์ขั้นต่ำแล้ว — ความปลอดภัยของพืชมาก่อน

วิธีเดียวกับตัวอย่างรถไฟฟ้าของอาจารย์: concern ยังเป็น NFR กว้าง ๆ จนกว่าจะถามต่อจนได้ function ที่มีเงื่อนไข ตัวเลข และการตอบสนองที่ทดสอบได้ ตัวเลขในคำตอบเป็นค่าสมมติที่ต้องยืนยันกับผู้เชี่ยวชาญด้านพืช และค่า EC เป็นตัววัดความเข้มข้นของสารละลาย ไม่ใช่ปริมาณน้ำ จึงไม่ใช้เป็นตัวบอกการขาดน้ำ

Q2Robotaxi. CityGo runs robotaxis in central Bangkok. Its enterprise goal: “be the robotaxi service passengers trust for safe, on-time trips.” Hint: consider safety and availability. Decompose the goal and declare functional requirements, including at least two quantitative NFRs. (5 marks)CityGo ให้บริการ robotaxi ใจกลางกรุงเทพฯ เป้าหมายองค์กรคือเป็นบริการที่ผู้โดยสารไว้ใจว่าปลอดภัยและตรงเวลา (hint: safety และ availability) จงแตก goal แล้วระบุ functional requirement พร้อม quantitative NFR อย่างน้อยสองข้อ

Use Lesson 8 · clause 6 and clause 1 (soft goal → hard goal)

Marker wants: goal → sub-goal → NFR → quantitative NFR, in order; numbers that can be tested; functional requirements derived from the hard goals, traceable to the enterprise goal.

Goal: ผู้โดยสารไว้ใจว่าเดินทางปลอดภัยและตรงเวลา → Sub-goals: (ก) ไม่มีอุบัติเหตุจากรถ (ข) รถมารับตรงเวลา (ค) ผู้โดยสารรู้สถานะและขอความช่วยเหลือได้

NFR: safety, availability, performance, usability → Quantitative NFR (ค่าสมมติ ต้องได้จาก benchmark และใช้ตรวจรับ): safety — เมื่อพบสิ่งกีดขวางในเส้นทาง รถต้องเริ่มเบรกภายใน 0.2 วินาที; availability — ระบบจองพร้อมใช้งาน 99.9% ระหว่าง 05:00–24:00; รถถึงจุดรับภายใน 8 นาทีสำหรับ 95% ของคำขอในเขตบริการ; ปุ่มฉุกเฉินต่อสายถึงเจ้าหน้าที่ภายใน 10 วินาที

Functional requirements จาก hard goal: (1) ระบบต้องแสดง ETA สดและอัปเดตทุก 10 วินาที (2) เมื่อเซนเซอร์สำคัญของรถผิดปกติ ระบบต้องจอดรถในจุดปลอดภัยและเรียก remote operator (3) ระบบต้องไม่เริ่มเดินทางถ้าประตูยังไม่ปิด (4) ปุ่ม emergency ต้องเปิดการสนทนากับเจ้าหน้าที่และส่งพิกัดรถ (5) ถ้ารถคันที่จองไว้ไม่พร้อม ระบบต้องจัดคันใหม่และแจ้งผู้โดยสารพร้อม ETA ใหม่

ประโยคปิดที่ได้คะแนน: ทุก requirement ตามรอยกลับไปหา goal ได้ — นี่คือข้อดีของ goal decomposition ตามสไลด์

Q3Requirement 7 and Thailand's PDPA are external facts. State what capabilities each one forces the Smart Farm system to have. (4 marks)ข้อ 7 (มาตรฐานรับรองของผู้ซื้อ) และ PDPA เป็นข้อเท็จจริงภายนอก จงระบุความสามารถที่ระบบต้องมีเพราะข้อเท็จจริงแต่ละข้อ

Use Lesson 8 · clause 5 (memo 1:07:50)

Marker wants: the fact restated; the part of the system it touches; a capability per fact written as something the system must store, check, exchange or keep, with a number where possible.

ข้อ 7 — การรับรองของผู้ซื้อ: ระบบต้อง (1) บันทึกการใช้สารเคมีและปุ๋ยทุกครั้งโดยผูกกับแปลง วันที่ และผู้บันทึก (2) เชื่อมบันทึกเหล่านั้นกับ lot ที่เกิดจากแปลงนั้น (3) เก็บอย่างน้อย 2 ปีนับจากวันเก็บเกี่ยว และห้ามลบหรือแก้ย้อนหลังโดยไม่มีประวัติ (4) ออกรายงานต่อ lot ให้ผู้ตรวจได้ภายในวันเดียว

PDPA: ระบบต้อง (1) เก็บข้อมูลส่วนบุคคลของคนงานและผู้ซื้อเท่าที่จำเป็นตามวัตถุประสงค์ (2) ขอความยินยอมก่อนเก็บและแจ้งวัตถุประสงค์ (3) ให้เจ้าของข้อมูลขอดูหรือขอลบได้ (4) จำกัดสิทธิ์เข้าถึงตาม role และหน้า QR ของผู้ซื้อต้องไม่แสดงข้อมูลส่วนบุคคล (ตรงกับข้อ 6)

สังเกตว่าทั้งสองข้อไม่ได้มาในรูป “The system shall…” — นักวิเคราะห์เป็นคนแปลงข้อเท็จจริงเป็นความสามารถ ซึ่งคือสิ่งที่อาจารย์บอกว่าจะถาม

Q4The owner will accept the alert and irrigation module only if functional adequacy X = 1 − A/B is at least 0.95, where A is the number of functions in which a problem is detected and B is the number of functions evaluated. Design the evaluation. (4 marks)เจ้าของจะตรวจรับโมดูล alert และรดน้ำก็ต่อเมื่อ X = 1 − A/B ≥ 0.95 จงออกแบบการทดสอบ: ค่า A และ B มาจากไหน เก็บข้อมูลอย่างไร และแปลผลอย่างไร

Use Lesson 8 · clause 10 · Video lab section 7 (the functional-adequacy calculation, 2:00:56)

Marker wants: the four steps — what is measured and why, the metric, how A and B are collected, how the result is judged.

(1) วัดอะไรเพื่อตอบอะไร: function ของโมดูล alert และรดน้ำทำงานถูกตามที่ผู้ใช้ต้องการแค่ไหน (ข้อ 3, 4, 9)

(2) ตัววัด: X = 1 − A/B

(3) เก็บข้อมูล: B = รายการ function ที่จะประเมิน เช่น 12 function — สร้าง alert เมื่อนอกช่วงเกิน 10 นาที, แจ้งผู้จัดการ, escalate หลัง 30 นาที, เปิด/ปิดวาล์วตามแผน, สั่งวาล์วเอง, บันทึกผู้สั่ง, ข้ามรดน้ำเมื่อฝน ≥ 70%, ไม่ข้ามเมื่อค่าต่ำกว่าเกณฑ์ ฯลฯ เขียน test case ต่อ function แล้วป้อนค่าเซนเซอร์จำลองผ่าน test harness ในสภาพแวดล้อม staging ผู้ทดสอบบันทึกผลแต่ละ case; A = จำนวน function ที่พบปัญหาอย่างน้อยหนึ่ง case

(4) แปลผล: ถ้าพบปัญหา 1 function จาก 12 ได้ X = 1 − 1/12 ≈ 0.92 < 0.95 → ยังไม่ผ่าน ต้องแก้แล้วทดสอบซ้ำ ค่ายิ่งใกล้ 1 ยิ่งดี อาจารย์ไม่ให้คิดตัววัดเอง แต่ให้ออกแบบว่าจะได้ A กับ B มาอย่างไร

Q5Before contracting a developer, GreenLeaf wants to validate the requirements. Most workers have little IT experience. Choose a validation technique and answer in the six-point frame: purpose, who is responsible, environment, input, steps, output. (5 marks)ก่อนจ้างผู้พัฒนา GreenLeaf ต้องการทำ requirements validation และคนงานส่วนใหญ่ใช้ IT ไม่คล่อง จงเลือกเทคนิคและตอบตามกรอบหกข้อ

Use Lesson 11 · clause 2, clause 3 · Lesson 10 · clause 3

Marker wants: one technique chosen with a reason tied to the case; all six points answered; steps in order; outputs that someone can act on.

เลือก prototyping สำหรับหน้าจอของคนงาน เพราะคนงานอ่าน SRS ไม่คล่อง แต่ตัดสินได้จากหน้าจอที่ลองกดจริง (เสริมด้วย requirements review ของ SRS สำหรับเจ้าของและผู้จัดการ)

กรอบคำตอบ
1 · ทำเพื่ออะไรตรวจว่า requirement ของการบันทึกการเก็บเกี่ยว งาน และวาล์วตรงกับวิธีทำงานจริง หาสิ่งที่ขาดหรือเข้าใจผิดก่อนทำสัญญา
2 · ใครรับผิดชอบrequirements engineer จัดและสังเกต; ผู้ทดสอบคือคนงานที่มีประสบการณ์และเปิดใจ ครบทุกโรงเรือน และผู้จัดการฟาร์ม
3 · สภาพแวดล้อมในโรงเรือนจริง ใช้แท็บเล็ตที่จะใช้งานจริง ช่วงเช้าก่อนงานเก็บเกี่ยว
4 · Inputprototype แบบกดได้ของหน้าจอหลัก, use case description, test scenario, checklist เกณฑ์ประเมิน และนิยาม defect type
5 · ขั้นตอนเลือกผู้ทดสอบ → เขียน scenario ที่ครอบคลุม (เช่น เก็บเกี่ยวแปลง READY, กรอกจำนวนเกิน, เน็ตหลุดตอนบันทึก) → ให้ผู้ใช้ทำเองโดย engineer สังเกตไม่ช่วย → บันทึกปัญหาและการเปลี่ยนแปลงที่ต้องทำ
6 · ผลลัพธ์รายการ defect พร้อมประเภท, requirement ที่ต้องแก้หรือเพิ่ม, รายงานการประเมิน และ requirement ที่ยืนยันแล้วพร้อมเป็น baseline

Q6Review these four requirements from the Smart Farm SRS. For each, name the defect type and the checklist group, and rewrite it.
